'''Healthcare in Canada''' is delivered through the provincial and territorial systems of [[Publicly funded health care|publicly funded]] [[single-payer healthcare]], informally called [[Medicare (Canada)|Medicare]].<ref name="AaseWaring2017">{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Jvs1DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA128 |title=Researching Quality in Care Transitions: International Perspectives |last1=Karina Aase |last2=Justin Waring |last3=Lene Schibevaag |publisher=Springer |year=2017 |isbn=978-3-319-62346-7 |pages=128–129}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news2/background/healthcare/public_vs_private.html |title=Public vs. private health care |date=December 1, 2006 |publisher=CBC News}}</ref> It is guided by the provisions of the ''[[Canada Health Act]], ''adopted during 1984,<ref name="Bégin1988">{{Cite book |title=Medicare: Canada's Right to Health |last=Monique Bégin |publisher=Optimum Pub. International |year=1988 |isbn=978-0-88890-219-1 |page=Intro}}</ref> and is [[Universal health care|universal]].<ref name="LeattMapa2003">{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2_y6J647QFoC&pg=PA81 |title=Government Relations in the Health Care Industry |last1=Peggy Leatt |last2=Joseph Mapa |publisher=Greenwood Publishing Group |year=2003 |isbn=978-1-56720-513-8}}</ref>{{rp|81}} The 2002 [[Royal Commission on the Future of Health Care in Canada|Royal Commission]], known as the Romanow Report, revealed that Canadians consider universal access to publicly funded health services as a "fundamental value that ensures national health care insurance for everyone wherever they live in the country".'''<ref name="Romanow_Report_2002">{{Cite report| first = Roy J. |last=Romanow | work = Government of Canada Public Services and Procurement Canada| title = Building on values: the future of health care in Canada |number=CP32–85/2002E–IN |isbn=0-662-33043-9 |page=392| access-date = January 9, 2021| location = Saskatoon| date = November 28, 2002| url = http://publications.gc.ca/collections/Collection/CP32-85-2002E.pdf }}</ref><ref name="Romanow_Recommendations_2002">{{Cite web |url=http://www.parl.gc.ca/content/sen/committee/372/soci/rep/repoct02vol6part7-e.htm |series=The Health of Canadians – The Federal Role |publisher=Parliament of Canada |location=17.2 Universality |language=en |access-date=January 5, 2017 |date=October 2002 |volume=6 |title=Recommendations for Reform}}</ref>'''

Canadian Medicare provides coverage for approximately 70 percent of Canadians' healthcare needs, and the remaining 30 percent is paid for through the private sector.<ref name="CIHI_2019"/><ref name="CIHI_2005"/> The 30 percent typically relates to services not covered or only partially covered by Medicare, such as [[prescription drug]]s, eye care, [[medical device]]s, [[Transgender health care|gender care]], [[psychotherapy]], [[physical therapy]] and [[Dentistry in Canada|dentistry]].<ref name="CIHI_2019"/><ref name="CIHI_2005"/> About 65-75 percent of Canadians have some form of supplementary [[health insurance]] related to the aforementioned reasons; many receive it through their employers or use secondary [[Social programs in Canada|social programs]] related to extended coverage for families receiving [[social assistance]] or vulnerable demographics, such as seniors, minors, and those with disabilities.<ref name="WaPo_20170701">{{Cite news| issn = 0190-8286| last = Kliff| first = Sarah| title = Everything you ever wanted to know about Canadian health care in one post| newspaper = [[The Washington Post]]| access-date = January 8, 2021 |date=July 1, 2017| url = https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/wonk/wp/2012/07/01/everything-you-ever-wanted-to-know-about-canadian-health-care-in-one-post/}}</ref>

According to the [[Canadian Institute for Health Information]] (CIHI), by 2019, Canada's [[aging population]] represents an increase in healthcare costs of approximately one percent a year, which is a modest increase. In a 2020 [[Statistics Canada]] Canadian Perspectives Survey Series (CPSS), 69 percent of Canadians self-reported that they had excellent or very good physical health—an improvement from 60 percent in 2018.<ref name="statcan_Findlay_20200424">{{Cite report| work = [[Statistics Canada]], Government of Canada|first1=Leanne |last1=Findlay |first2=Rubab |last2=Arim| title = Canadians report lower self-perceived mental health during the COVID-19 pandemic| access-date = January 9, 2021| date = April 24, 2020| url = https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/pub/45-28-0001/2020001/article/00003-eng.htm}}</ref> In 2019, 80 percent of Canadian adults self-reported having at least one major risk factor for chronic disease: [[Smoking in Canada|smoking]], physical inactivity, unhealthy eating, or excessive [[Alcoholic drinks in Canada|alcohol]] use.<ref name="GregoryStephens2019">{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uEeCDwAAQBAJ&pg=PT75 |title=Fundamentals: Perspectives on the Art and Science of Canadian Nursing |last1=David Gregory |last2=Tracey Stephens |last3=Christy Raymond-Seniuk |last4=Linda Patrick |publisher=Wolters Kluwer Health |year=2019 |isbn=978-1-4963-9850-5 |page=75}}</ref> Canada has [[Obesity in Canada|one of the highest rates of adult obesity]] among [[OECD|Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development]] (OECD) countries attributing to approximately 2.7 million cases of [[diabetes]] (types 1 and 2 combined).<ref name="GregoryStephens2019" /> Four chronic diseases—[[cancer]] (a leading cause of death), [[cardiovascular disease]]s, [[respiratory disease]]s and diabetes account for 65 percent of deaths in Canada.<ref name="GregoryStephens2019" /> There are approximately 8 million individuals aged 15 and older with one or more [[Disability in Canada|disabilities in Canada]].<ref name="k471">{{cite web | title=The Daily — Canadian Survey on Disability, 2017 to 2022 | website=Statistics Canada | date=2023-12-01 | url=https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/daily-quotidien/231201/dq231201b-eng.htm | access-date=2025-01-05}}</ref>

In 2021, the [[Canadian Institute for Health Information]] reported that [[Health spending as percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by country|healthcare spending]] reached $308{{nbsp}}billion, or 12.7 percent of Canada's GDP for that year.<ref>{{cite web |year=2022 |title=National Health Expenditure Trends|url=https://www.cihi.ca/en/national-health-expenditure-trends|access-date=August 23, 2022|publisher=Canadian Institute for Health Information}}</ref> In 2022 Canada's per-capita spending on [[List of countries by total health expenditure per capita|health expenditures]] ranked 12th among [[List of countries by total health expenditure per capita|healthcare systems in the OECD]].<ref name=OECD-barcharts/> Canada has performed close to the average on the majority of OECD health indicators since the early 2000s,<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.oecd.org/canada/Health-at-a-Glance-2017-Key-Findings-CANADA.pdf |title=Health at a Glance 2017 |year=2017 |publisher=OECD Publishing}}</ref> and ranks above average for [[Universal health care|access to care]], but the number of doctors and hospital beds are considerably below the OECD average.<ref name="OECD_2017"/> The [[Commonwealth Fund]]s 2021 report comparing the healthcare systems of 11 high-income countries ranked Canada second-to-last.<ref name="auto3">{{Cite journal|url=https://www.commonwealthfund.org/publications/fund-reports/2021/aug/mirror-mirror-2021-reflecting-poorly|title=Mirror, Mirror 2021: Reflecting Poorly|date=August 4, 2021|website=www.commonwealthfund.org|doi=10.26099/01dv-h208 |last1=Schneider |first1=Eric C. |last2=Shah |first2=Arnav |last3=Doty |first3=Michelle M. |author4=Roosa Tikkanen |last5=Fields |first5=Katharine |last6=Williams II |first6=Reginald D. }}</ref> Identified weaknesses of Canada's system were comparatively higher infant mortality rate, the prevalence of chronic conditions, long wait times, poor availability of after-hours care, and a lack of prescription drugs coverage.<ref name="Prescription for Canada">A Prescription for Canada:  Achieving Pharmacare for All (Government of Canada report, retrieved 2023)</ref> An increasing problem in Canada's health system is a shortage of [[Health professional|healthcare professionals]] and hospital capacity.<ref name="Duong Vogel 2023 pp. E309–E310">{{cite journal | last1=Duong | first1=Diana | last2=Vogel | first2=Lauren | title=Overworked health workers are "past the point of exhaustion" | journal=Canadian Medical Association Journal | publisher=CMA Impact Inc. | volume=195 | issue=8 | date=2023-02-26 | issn=0820-3946 | doi=10.1503/cmaj.1096042 | pages=E309–E310| pmid=36849179 | pmc=9970629 }}</ref><ref name="Thiessen Partner Organization Ma 2023 j399">{{cite web |title=Taking the pulse: A snapshot of Canadian health care, 2023 | website=[[Canadian Institute for Health Information]]| date=August 2, 2023 | url=https://www.cihi.ca/en/book/export/html/10799 | access-date=February 15, 2024}}</ref>

==Canadian healthcare policy==
The primary objective of the Canadian healthcare policy, as set out in the 1984 [[Canada Health Act]] (CHA), is to "protect, promote and restore the physical and mental well-being of residents of Canada and to facilitate reasonable access to health services without financial or other barriers."<ref name="CHA_1984">{{cite web|title=Canada Health Act|publisher=Government of Canada|date=April 1, 1984|url=https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/c-6/index.html |number=R.S.C. 1985, c. C-6, s. 3| access-date = January 8, 2021}}</ref><ref name="LoP_Tiedemann_20191217">{{Cite web| title = The Canada Health Act: An Overview| access-date = January 8, 2021| url = https://lop.parl.ca/sites/PublicWebsite/default/en_CA/ResearchPublications/201954E? |first=Marlisa |last=Tiedemann |work=Library of Parliament |series=Research publications |number= 2019–54–E |page=18 |date=December 17, 2019}}</ref> The federal government ensures compliance with its requirements that all Canadians have "reasonable access to medically necessary hospital, physician, and surgical-dental services that require a hospital" by providing cash to provinces and territories through the [[Canada Health Transfer]] (CHT) based on their fulfilling certain "criteria and conditions related to insured health services and extended health care services."<ref name="LoP_Tiedemann_20191217"/>

In his widely cited 1987 book, Malcolm G. Taylor traced the roots of Medicare and federal-provincial negotiations involving "issues of jurisdiction, cost allocations, revenue transfers, and taxing authorities" that resulted in the current system that provides healthcare to "Canadians on the basis of need, irrespective of financial circumstances."<ref name="Taylor_1987">{{Cite book| last1 = Taylor| first1 = Malcolm G. | title = Health Insurance and Canadian Public Policy: The Seven Decisions That Created the Health Insurance System and Their Outcomes| date = 1987 |edition=2 |publisher=McGill Queen's University Press |location=Kingston and Montreal}}</ref><ref name="Taylor_2009">{{Cite book| isbn = 978-0-7735-3566-4| last1 = Taylor| first1 = Malcolm G. |first2=Allan |last2=Maslove| title = Health Insurance and Canadian Public Policy: The Seven Decisions That Created the Health Insurance System and Their Outcomes| date = April 1, 2009| jstor = j.ctt80w3s |publisher=McGill Queen's University Press (MQUP) |orig-date=1987|page=579}}</ref>

==Monitoring and measuring healthcare in Canada==
Health Canada, under the direction of the Health Minister, is the ministry responsible for overseeing Canada's healthcare, including its public policies and implementations. This includes the maintenance and improvement of the health of the Canadian population, which is "among the healthiest in the world as measured by longevity, lifestyle and effective use of the public health care system."<ref name="CHA_2015">{{cite report |location=Ottawa, Ontario |date=2015 |publisher=Minister of Health |title=Annual Report 2014-2015}}</ref>

[[Health Canada]], a [[structure of the Canadian federal government|federal department]], publishes a series of surveys of the healthcare system in Canada.<ref name="Canadastat">{{Cite web|title=Healthy Canadians: Canadian government report on comparable health care indicators|date=July 2002|url=https://publications.gc.ca/site/eng/9.506140/publication.html|access-date=December 6, 2021}}</ref> Although life-threatening cases are dealt with immediately, some services needed are non-urgent and patients are seen at the next-available appointment in their local chosen facility.

In 1996, in response to an interest in renewing its healthcare system, the federal government established the Canadian Health Services Research Foundation (CHRSF) in the 1996 federal budget to conduct research in collaboration with "provincial governments, health institutions, and the private sector" to identify the successes and failures in the health system.<ref name="Mullner_2009">{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MUItoTour5oC&q=Canada+Health+Act&pg=PA559 |title=Encyclopedia of health services research |last=Mullner |first=Ross M |publisher=SAGE |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-4129-7194-2 |pages=559–562}}</ref>{{rp|113}}

The [[Canadian Institute for Health Information]] (CIHI) is a not-for-profit, independent organization established by the provincial, territorial, and federal government to make healthcare information publicly available.<ref name="about_CIHI">{{citation |url=http://www.statcan.gc.ca/pub/82-221-x/2011002/abc-eng.htm |title=About the Canadian Institute for Health Information' |work=Statistics Canada |date=October 25, 2011}}</ref> The CIHI was established in 1994 to serve as a national "coordinating council and an independent institute for health information" in response to the 1991 report, "Health Information for Canada" produced by the National Task Force on Health Information.<ref name="CIHI_History_2019">{{Cite web| title = CIHI: A history| access-date =January 8, 2021 |work=[[Canadian Institute for Health Information]]| url = https://www.cihi.ca/en/cihi-a-history}}</ref> In 1994, the CIHI merged the Hospital Medical Records Institute (HMRI) and The Management Information Systems (MIS) Group.<ref name="CIHI_History_2019"/>

Reports include topics such as the evaluating and suggested improvements for the efficiency of healthcare services. Regions that were similar in factors such as education levels and immigration numbers were found to have different efficiency levels in health care provision. The study concluded if increased efficiency of the current system was set as a goal, the death rate could be decreased by 18%-35%.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Health System Efficiency in Canada: Why Does Efficiency Vary Among Regions?|url=https://secure.cihi.ca/free_products/hse_short_aib_10apr14_en.pdf|access-date=December 6, 2021|website=www.cihi.ca|publisher=Canadian Institute for Health Information}}</ref> The study notes that supporting physician leadership and facilitating engagement of the care providers could reap great gains in efficiency. Additionally, the study suggested facilitating the exchange of information and interaction between health providers and government figures as well as flexible funding would also contribute to the improvement and solve the problem of differences in regional care by allowing regions to determine the needs of their general populace and meet those needs more efficiently by allowing target-specific allocation of funds.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://secure.cihi.ca/free_products/improving_health_system_efficiency_en.pdf |title=Improving Health System Efficiency in Canada Perspectives of Decision-Makers |website=secure.cihi.ca |publisher=Canadian Institute for Health Information |access-date=December 13, 2018}}</ref>

For 24 years, the CIHI has produced an annual detailed report updating "National Health Expenditure Trends" which includes data tables with the most recent report published in January 2021.<ref name="CIHI_upcoming">{{Cite web| title = Upcoming releases |work= [[Canadian Institute for Health Information]] CIHI| access-date = January 8, 2021| url = https://www.cihi.ca/en/upcoming-releases}}</ref><ref name="CIHI_Trends_2019"/> Other CIHI research topics include hospital care, organ and joint replacements, health system performance, seniors and aging, health workforce, health inequality, quality and safety, mental health and addictions, pharmaceuticals, international comparisons, emergency care, patient experience, residential care, population health, community care, patient outcomes, access and wait times, children and youth, and First Nations, Inuit and Métis.

In 2003, at the First Ministers' Accord on Health Care Renewal, the [[Health Council of Canada]] (HCC)—an independent national agency—was established to monitor and report on Canada's healthcare system.<ref name="HCC_seniors_201204">{{cite web|last=Kitts|first=Jack|date=April 2012|title=Seniors in need, caregivers in distress: What are the home care priorities for seniors in Canada?|url=http://zweb-s3.uploads.s3.amazonaws.com/carp/2012/04/HCC_HomeCare_2d.pdf|access-date=December 6, 2021|quote="Created by the 2003 First Ministers' Accord on Health Care Renewal, the Health Council of Canada is an independent national agency that reports on the progress of health care renewal. The Council provides a system wide perspective on health care reform in Canada, and disseminates information on leading practices and innovation across the country. The Councillors are appointed by the participating provincial and territorial governments and the Government of Canada."}}</ref> For over a decade, until 2014, the HCC produced 60 reports on access and wait times, health promotion, seniors healthcare, aboriginal healthcare, home and community care, pharmaceuticals management, and primary health care.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.healthcouncilcanada.ca/content.php?mnu=2&mnu1=36|title=HCC reports|access-date=October 18, 2020|archive-date=August 4, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170804095442/http://healthcouncilcanada.ca/content.php?mnu=2&mnu1=36}}</ref>

==Demographics==
[[File:A snapshot of the health of Canadians-eng.jpg|upright=1.1|thumb|A snapshot of the health of Canadians]]
By February 2024, the median age in Canada was 40.6 years in 2023<ref name="statcan_20242102">{{Cite web |last=Government of Canada |first=Statistics Canada |date=Feb 21, 2024 |title=Population estimates on July 1, by age and gender |url=https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/t1/tbl1/en/tv.action?pid=1710000501 |access-date=February 28, 2024 |website=Statistics Canada}}</ref> compared to 39.5 in 2006.<ref name="statscan_2006">{{Cite web|last1=Martel|first1=Laurent|last2=Malenfant, Éric Caron|date=September 22, 2009|title=2006 Census: Portrait of the Canadian Population in 2006, by Age and Sex|url=https://www12.statcan.gc.ca/census-recensement/2006/as-sa/97-551/index-eng.cfm|access-date=December 6, 2021|publisher=Statistics Canada}}</ref>

By July 2020, there were 6,835,866 individuals who were 65 years old and older and 11,517 [[centenarian]]s.<ref name="statcan_20190208">{{Cite web| last = Government of Canada| first = Statistics Canada| title = Seniors and aging statistics| access-date = January 9, 2021| date = February 2, 2019| url = https://www.statcan.gc.ca/eng/subjects-start/seniors_and_aging| archive-date = January 11, 2021| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210111221101/https://www.statcan.gc.ca/eng/subjects-start/seniors_and_aging}}</ref> The same data reported that by July 2020, 16% of Canadians were 14-years-old or under, 66.5% were between the ages of 15 and 65, and 17.5% were 65 years and older.<ref name="statcan_20190208"/>

Canada's population is aging, like that of many other countries.<ref name="statscan_health&aging_20160728">{{Cite report |date=October 30, 2015 |series=Presentation to the National Statistics Council |first=Claudia |last=Sanmartin| work = Statistics Canada, Government of Canada| title = Research Highlights on Health and Aging| access-date = October 17, 2020| url = https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/pub/11-631-x/11-631-x2016001-eng.htm}}</ref> By 2016, there were about six million seniors in Canada, which then had a population of approximately 34 million.<ref name="CMA_stateofseniorshealth_2016">{{Cite web |url=https://www.cma.ca/En/Lists/Medias/the-state-of-seniors-health-care-in-canada-september-2016.pdf |title=The State of Seniors Healthcare in Canada |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171213191639/https://www.cma.ca/En/Lists/Medias/the-state-of-seniors-health-care-in-canada-september-2016.pdf |archive-date=December 13, 2017}}</ref> This significantly influences Canada's healthcare services;<ref name="statscan_health&aging_20160728"/> by 2019, Canada's aging population represented a modest increase in healthcare costs of about 1% a year.<ref name="CIHI_2019">{{Cite web |last=K |first=N |date=November 7, 2024 |title=Health spending in Canada reaches $264 billion |url=https://www.cihi.ca/en/national-health-expenditure-trends |access-date=January 11, 2025 |work=[[Canadian Institute for Health Information]]}}</ref>

Since the 2010s, Statistics Canada health research on aging has focused on "chronic diseases," "social isolation" and senior's mental health needs, and "transitions to institutional care" including long-term care.<ref name="statscan_health&aging_20160728"/> The eight chronic conditions that are prevalent in one out of ten seniors include high blood pressure, arthritis, back problems, eye problems, heart disease, osteoporosis, diabetes and urinary incontinence, with many seniors having [[Multimorbidity|multiple chronic conditions]].<ref name="statscan_health&aging_20160728"/> Those with chronic conditions are "associated with higher use of home-care services and need for formal-care providers."<ref name="statscan_health&aging_20160728"/>

Ninety percent of Canadians agree that Canada should have a "national seniors strategy to address needs along the full continuum of care."<ref name="CMA_stateofseniorshealth_2016"/>
==Current status==
The government guarantees the quality of care through federal standards. The government does not participate in day-to-day care or collect any information about an individual's health, which remains confidential between a person and their physician.<ref name="theglobeandmail.com">{{Cite news |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/globe-debate/five-things-canadians-get-wrong-about-the-health-system/article20360452/ |title=Five things Canadians get wrong about the health system |work=The Globe and Mail}}</ref> In each province, each doctor handles the insurance claim against the provincial insurer. There is no need for the person who accesses healthcare to be involved in billing and reclaim. In 2005, Private health expenditure accounts for 30% of health care financing.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://secure.cihi.ca/free_products/FundRep_EN.pdf |title=Exploring the 70/30 Split: How Canada's Health Care System Is Financed |publisher=The Canadian Institute for Health Information |access-date=April 11, 2013 |archive-date=January 30, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190130002757/https://secure.cihi.ca/free_products/FundRep_EN.pdf }}</ref>

The ''[[Canada Health Act]]'' does not cover prescription drugs, home care, or long-term care or [[Dentistry|dental care]].<ref name="theglobeandmail.com" /> Provinces provide partial coverage for children, those living in poverty, and seniors.<ref name="theglobeandmail.com" /> Programs vary by province. In Ontario, for example, most prescriptions for youths under the age of 24 are covered by the Ontario health insurance plan if no private insurance plan is available.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ontario.ca/page/learn-about-ohip-plus |title=Learn about OHIP+ |date=July 4, 2017 |publisher=Ontario Ministry of Health |access-date=July 7, 2021 }}</ref>

As of 2024, Canada introduced the Canadian Dental Care Plan (CDCP), aimed at expanding access to dental services for eligible citizens. The plan is being rolled out in phases, beginning with seniors, children under 18, and people with disabilities who lack private dental insurance and have a household income under $90,000. This federal initiative marks a significant shift in addressing dental care affordability and access, complementing the varying levels of provincial support already in place.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.canada.ca/en/services/benefits/dental/dental-care-plan.html |title=Canadian Dental Care Plan |date=December 8, 2023 |publisher=Government of Canada |access-date=May 11, 2025 }}</ref>

Competitive practices such as advertising are kept to a minimum, thus maximizing the percentage of revenues that go directly towards care. Costs are paid through funding from federal and provincial general tax revenues, which include income taxes, sales taxes, and corporate taxes. In British Columbia, taxation-based funding was (until January 1, 2020) supplemented by a fixed monthly premium that was waived or reduced for those on low incomes.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/health/health-drug-coverage/msp/bc-residents/msp-premium-elimination-jan-1-2020|title=Ministry of Health - Redirect|website=gov.bc.ca}}</ref> In Ontario, there is an income tax identified as a health premium on taxable income above $20,000.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.ontario.ca/page/health-premium |title=Health Premium |date=February 21, 2018 |publisher=Queen's Printer for Ontario |access-date=February 19, 2019}}</ref>

In addition to funding through the tax system, hospitals and medical research are funded in part by charitable contributions. For example, in 2018, Toronto's [[The Hospital for Sick Children (Toronto)|Hospital for Sick Children]] embarked on campaign to raise $1.3 billion to equip a new hospital.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.ctvnews.ca/canada/article/sickkids-hospital-rallying-crews-around-13-billion-fundraising-drive/ |title=SickKids hospital rallying 'crews' around $1.3-billion fundraising drive  |work=CTV News |date=October 9, 2018 |access-date=February 19, 2019}}</ref> Charities such as the [[Canadian Cancer Society]] provide assistance such as transportation for patients.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.cancer.ca/en/support-and-services/support-services/travel-and-accommodations-on/?region=on |title=Travel and accommodation - Canadian Cancer Society |website=www.cancer.ca |access-date=February 19, 2019}}</ref> There are no deductibles on basic health care and co-pays are extremely low or non-existent (supplemental insurance such as Fair [[Pharmacare]] may have deductibles, depending on income). In general, user fees are not permitted by the ''Canada Health Act'', but physicians may charge a small fee to the patient for reasons such as missed appointments, doctor's notes, and prescription refills done over the phone. Some physicians charge "annual fees" as part of a comprehensive package of services they offer their patients and their families. Legally, such charges must be completely optional and can only be for non-essential health options,<ref name="theglobeandmail.com" /> however, some clinics have allegedly broken these rules,<ref>{{Cite news |last=Lindsay |first=Bethany |date=June 12, 2017 |title=Private B.C. clinics accused of charging patients improper fees |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/private-healthcare-clinics-user-fees-1.4157288 |access-date=August 1, 2024 |work=CBC News}}</ref> and provincial agencies have pursued injunctions and investigations.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bowman |first=Martin MacMahon, Greg |date=2023-04-26 |title=Telus ditches fee-based doctor program in BC |url=https://vancouver.citynews.ca/2023/04/26/telus-health-ditches-paid-doctor-program/ |access-date=2024-08-01 |website=CityNews Vancouver}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=DeRosa |first=Katie |date=February 7, 2023 |title=B.C.'s medical services watchdog sues Vancouver clinic, alleging illegal extra billing |url=https://vancouversun.com/news/local-news/medical-services-watchdog-sues-vancouver-clinic-alleging-illegal-extra-billing |archive-url=https://archive.today/20230208155610/https://vancouversun.com/news/local-news/medical-services-watchdog-sues-vancouver-clinic-alleging-illegal-extra-billing |archive-date=February 8, 2023 |access-date=August 1, 2024 |work=The Vancouver Sun}}</ref>

===Benefits and features===
Health cards are issued by provincial health ministries to individuals who enroll for the program, though newcomers must wait up to three months after they arrive in the province,<ref>{{Cite news |date=2016-10-24 |title=Home-care coverage gap remains for patients who move provinces |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/national/home-care-coverage-gap-remains-for-patients-who-move-provinces/article32489673/ |access-date=2024-08-01 |work=The Globe and Mail |language=en-CA}}</ref> and everyone receives the same level of care once they receive one.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.hc-sc.gc.ca/hcs-sss/delivery-prestation/ptrole/index-eng.php |title=Provincial/Territorial Role in Health |date=August 23, 2016 |website=Hc-sc.gc.ca}}</ref> Most essential basic care is covered, including maternity but excluding [[mental health]] and [[home care]].<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/philpott-provinces-hit-impasse-over-health-funding/article32434450/ |title=Philpott, provinces hit impasse over health funding |access-date=May 27, 2018 |work=The Globe and Mail}}</ref> [[Infertility]] costs are not covered in any province other than Quebec, though they are now partially covered in some other provinces.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://business.financialpost.com/2013/09/28/does-your-province-cover-the-cost-of-infertility-treatments/ |title=Does your province cover the cost of infertility treatments? |last=Melissa Leong |date=September 28, 2013 |website=Financial Post}}</ref> In some provinces, private supplemental plans are available for those who desire private rooms if they are hospitalized. [[Cosmetic Surgery|Cosmetic surgery]] and some forms of elective surgery are not considered essential care and are generally not covered. For example, Canadian health insurance plans do not cover non-therapeutic [[circumcision]].<ref name="bulletin">{{Cite journal|year=2005|title=PSHCP Bulletin 17|url=https://www.pshcp.ca/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/bulletin17EN.pdf|journal=The Public Service Health Care Plan Bulletin|issue=17|page=2}}</ref> These can be paid out-of-pocket or through private insurers.

Basic health coverage is not affected by loss or change of jobs, cannot be denied due to unpaid premiums, and is not subject to lifetime limits or exclusions for pre-existing conditions. The ''Canada Health Act'' deems that essential physician and hospital care be covered by the publicly funded system, but each province has reasons to determine what is considered essential, and where, how and who should provide the services. There are some provinces that are moving towards private health care away from public health care.{{Citation needed|date=December 2022}} The result is that there is a wide variance in what is covered across the country by the public health system, particularly in more controversial or expensive areas, such as mental health, substance use treatment, [[in-vitro fertilization]],<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://globalnews.ca/news/3059988/paying-to-treat-infertility-coverage-varies-widely-across-canada/ |title=Paying to treat infertility: Coverage varies widely across Canada - National {{!}} Globalnews.ca |date=November 15, 2016 |website=globalnews.ca |access-date=February 19, 2019}}</ref> [[sex reassignment surgery|gender-affirming surgery]],<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/prince-edward-island/pei-health-gender-constructive-surgeries-1.4655251 |title=P.E.I. to cover gender reconstructive surgeries|last=Harding |first=Gail|website=CBC |access-date=February 19, 2019}}</ref> or [[autism]] treatments.<ref name="theglobeandmail.com" />

Canada (with the exception of the province of [[Quebec]]) is one of the few countries with a universal healthcare system that does not include coverage of prescription medication (other such countries are Russia and some of the former USSR republics<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.kp.ru/online/news/2736284/ |title=Russia may introduce free prescription drugs |date=May 5, 2017}}</ref>). Residents of Quebec who are covered by the province's public prescription drug plan pay an annual premium of $0 to $660 when they file their Quebec income tax return.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://umanitoba.ca/outreach/evidencenetwork/archives/11837 |title=Canadian medicare needs an Rx |website=umanitoba.ca |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141220025027/http://umanitoba.ca/outreach/evidencenetwork/archives/11837 |archive-date=December 20, 2014 |access-date=September 19, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.thestar.com/opinion/editorialopinion/2012/10/09/why_in_a_sea_of_pink_are_so_many_cancer_patients_in_the_red.html |title=Why, in a sea of pink, are so many cancer patients in the red? |date=October 9, 2012 |website=thestar.com}}</ref>

Over the past two decades, at least some provinces have introduced some universal prescription drug insurance. Nova Scotia has Family Pharmacare, introduced in 2008 by Rodney MacDonald's Progressive Conservative government.<ref>{{Cite press release |title=New Nova Scotia Family Pharmacare Program Begins |publisher=Government of Nova Scotia |url=https://novascotia.ca/news/release/?id=20080303004 |access-date=June 17, 2019 |website=novascotia.ca}}</ref> However, residents do not automatically receive it through their health care as they must register separately for it, and it covers a limited range of prescriptions. No premiums are charged. A deductible and out-of-pocket maximum for copayments are set as a percentage of taxable income of two years before.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://novascotia.ca/dhw/pharmacare/family-pharmacare.asp |title=Family Pharmacare Program |website=novascotia.ca |publisher=Government of Nova Scotia |access-date=June 17, 2019}}</ref>

Pharmaceutical medications are covered by public funds in some provinces for the elderly or indigent,<ref>CIHI p.91</ref> through employment-based private insurance or paid for out-of-pocket. In Ontario, eligible medications are provided at no cost for covered individuals aged 24 and under.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.health.gov.on.ca/en/pro/programs/drugs/ohipplus/#covered |title=OHIP+: Children and Youth Pharmacare |publisher=Queen's Printer for Ontario |access-date=February 19, 2019}}</ref> Most drug prices are negotiated with suppliers by each provincial government to control costs but more recently, the [[Council of the Federation]] announced an initiative for select provinces to work together to create a larger buying block for more leverage to control costs of pharmaceutical drugs.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.conseildelafederation.ca/en/initiatives/358-pan-canadian-pricing-alliance |title=Canada's Premiers - The pan-Canadian Pharmaceutical Alliance |last=Cara |website=conseildelafederation.ca |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141220024057/http://www.conseildelafederation.ca/en/initiatives/358-pan-canadian-pricing-alliance |archive-date=December 20, 2014 |access-date=September 19, 2014}}</ref> More than 60 percent of prescription medications are paid for privately in Canada.<ref name="theglobeandmail.com" /> [[Family physician]]s ("General Practitioners") are assigned to individuals using provincial waitlist registry systems.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Health Connect Registry {{!}} HealthLink BC |url=https://www.healthlinkbc.ca/health-connect-registry |access-date=2024-08-01 |website=www.healthlinkbc.ca}}</ref> If a patient wishes to see a specialist or is counseled to see a specialist by their GP, a referral is made by a GP in the local community. Preventive care and early detection are considered critical.{{Citation needed|date=December 2022}}

==Coverage==
===Mental health===
The ''Canada Health Act'' covers the services of [[psychiatrist]]s, [[medical doctors]] with additional training in [[psychiatry]]. In Canada, psychiatrists tend to focus on the treatment of mental illness with medication.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://opajoomla.knowledge4you.ca/index.php/getting-help-faq/psychologistpsychiatrist |title=Frequently Asked Questions: What is the difference between a psychologist and a psychiatrist? |publisher=The Ontario Psychological Association |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150130212214/http://opajoomla.knowledge4you.ca/index.php/getting-help-faq/psychologistpsychiatrist |archive-date=January 30, 2015 |access-date=January 30, 2015 |quote=The practice of most psychiatrists in Ontario is focused on prescribing medications and consulting with family physicians, psychologists and other health professionals.}}</ref> However, the ''Canada Health Act'' excludes care provided in a "hospital or institution primarily for the mentally disordered."<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://ww1.cpa-apc.org/Publications/Archives/Bulletin/2004/february/newsCHAen.asp |title=Canada Health Act Exclusion of Certain Psychiatric Services Draws Attention |publisher=Canadian Psychiatric Association |access-date=January 30, 2015}}</ref> Some institutional care is provided by provinces. The ''Canada Health Act'' does not cover treatment by a [[psychologist]]<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://opajoomla.knowledge4you.ca/index.php/getting-help-faq/who-pays |title=Frequently Asked Questions: Who pays for psychological treatment? |publisher=The Ontario Psychological Association |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150130192656/http://opajoomla.knowledge4you.ca/index.php/getting-help-faq/who-pays |archive-date=January 30, 2015 |access-date=January 30, 2015}}</ref> or [[psychotherapist]] unless the practitioner is also a medical doctor. [[Goods and Services Tax (Canada)|Goods and Services Tax]] or [[Harmonized Sales Tax]] (depending on the province) applies to the services of psychotherapists.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.psychotherapyontario.org/prOSPect/OSPprOSPectSpring2010.pdf |title=HST Update |publisher=Ontario Society of Psychotherapists |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150201022406/http://www.psychotherapyontario.org/prOSPect/OSPprOSPectSpring2010.pdf |archive-date=February 1, 2015 |access-date=January 30, 2015}}</ref> Some coverage for mental health care and substance abuse treatment may be available under other government programs. For example, in Alberta, the province provides funding for mental health care through Alberta Health Services.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.health.alberta.ca/AHCIP/what-is-covered.html |title=What is covered under the AHCIP |publisher=Alberta Health |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150130192755/http://www.health.alberta.ca/AHCIP/what-is-covered.html |archive-date=January 30, 2015 |access-date=January 30, 2015}}</ref> Most or all provinces and territories offer government-funded drug and alcohol addiction rehabilitation, although waiting lists may exist.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.drugrehab.ca/directory.html |title=Directory [of drug rehab centers by province] |publisher=Drug Rehab Services (a nonprofit organization) |access-date=January 19, 2017}}</ref> The cost of treatment by a psychologist or psychotherapist in Canada has been cited as a contributing factor in the high suicide rate among first responders such as police officers, [[Emergency medical technician|EMTs]] and [[paramedic]]s. According to a CBC report, some police forces "offer benefits plans that cover only a handful of sessions with community psychologists, forcing those seeking help to join lengthy waiting lists to seek free psychiatric assistance."<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/ottawa/troubled-cops-need-more-government-help-mental-health-experts-say-1.2788319 |title=Troubled cops need more government help, mental health experts say |date=October 5, 2014 |publisher=CBC |access-date=February 1, 2015}}</ref>

===Oral health===
Among the OECD countries, Canada ranks second to last in the public funding of [[oral health]]care.{{citation needed|date=February 2020}} Those who need dental care are usually responsible for the finances and some may benefit from the coverage available through employment, under provincial plans, or private dental care plans. "As opposed to its national system of public health insurance, dental care in Canada is almost wholly privately financed, with approximately 60% of dental care paid through employment-based insurance, and 35% through out-of-pocket expenditures. Of the approximately 5% of publicly financed care that remains, most has focused on socially marginalized groups (e.g., low-income children and adults), and is supported by different levels of government depending on the group insured."<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Quiñonez, Carlos |last2=Grootendorst, Paul |year=2011 |title=Equity in dental care among Canadian households |journal=International Journal for Equity in Health |volume=10 |page=14 |doi=10.1186/1475-9276-10-14 |pmc=3097153 |pmid=21496297 |doi-access=free }}</ref> It is true that compared to primary care checkups, dental care checkups depend on the ability of people being able to pay those fees.

Studies in Quebec and Ontario provide data on the extent of dental health care.{{Citation needed|date=December 2022}} For example, studies in Quebec showed that there was a strong relation among dental services and the socioeconomic factors of income and education whereas in Ontario older adults heavily relied on dental insurance with visits to the dentist. "According to the National Public Health Service in 1996 / 1997, it showed a whopping difference of people who were in different classes. About half of Canadians aged 15 or older (53%) reported having dental insurance. Coverage tended to be highest among middle-aged people. At older ages, the rate dropped, and only one-fifth of the 65-or-older age group (21%) was covered."<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.statcan.gc.ca/pub/82-003-x/1999001/article/4646-eng.pdf |title=Dental Insurance and use of Dental Services |website=Statcan.gc.ca |access-date=May 27, 2018}}</ref> Attributes that can contribute to these outcomes is household income, employment, as well as education. Those individuals who are in the middle class may be covered through the benefits of their employment whereas older individuals may not due to the fact of retirement.

Under the government healthcare system in Canada, routine dental care is not covered.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Canada's Health Care System|url=https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/health-care-system/reports-publications/health-care-system/canada.html|access-date=December 21, 2020|website=Government of Canada|date=May 26, 2011|archive-date=December 19, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201219230725/https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/health-care-system/reports-publications/health-care-system/canada.html}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Are Dental Implants Covered by Insurance in Canada?|url=https://nvwelldental.com/are-dental-implants-covered-by-insurance-in-canada/|access-date=December 21, 2020|website=Smile Well Dental|date=April 22, 2020}}</ref> There are a couple of provinces that offer child prevention programs such as Nova Scotia and Quebec.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Government Dental Programs|url=http://www.caphd.ca/programs-and-resources/government-dental-programs|access-date=December 21, 2020|website=Canadian Association of Public Health Dentistry}}</ref> Other provinces make patients pay for medical dental procedures that are performed in the hospital. Some dental services that are possibly not covered by Medicare may include cavity fillings, routine dental check-ups, restorative dental care, and preventive care, dentures, dental implants, bridges, crowns, veneers, and in-lays, X-rays, and orthodontic procedures.

In 2022, however, the federal government announced the creation of a new Canada Dental Benefit which reimburses low- to middle-income parents up to $650 of dental fees per child.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Agency |first=Canada Revenue |date=2022-09-20 |title=Canada Dental Benefit |url=https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/child-family-benefits/dental-benefit.html |access-date=2022-12-20 |website=www.canada.ca}}</ref> This was a transitional policy on the way to universal, public coverage of dental care. In 2023, the government established the [[Canadian Dental Care Plan]], which began a staggered enrolment rollout in December 2023, to pay costs for covered dental services of eligible residents.<ref name="Rachini">{{cite web|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/canada-dental-care-plan-benefit-1.7055975|title=Canada's new dental care plan could impact nearly 9 million Canadians — are you one of them?|last=Rachini|first=Mouhamad|publisher=[[CBC News]]|date=12 December 2023|access-date=31 January 2024}}</ref>

===Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and massage therapy===
Coverage for services by [[physiotherapist]]s, [[occupational therapist]]s (also known as OTs) and Registered [[Massage Therapist]]s (RMTs) varies by province. For example, in Ontario the provincial health plan, OHIP, does cover physiotherapy following hospital discharge and occupational therapy<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pthealth.ca/service/occupational-therapy/ |title=Occupational Therapy (OT) |publisher=pt Health |access-date=January 19, 2017}}</ref> but does not cover massage therapy. To be eligible for coverage for physiotherapy in Ontario, insured individuals must have been discharged as an inpatient of a hospital after an overnight stay and require physiotherapy for the condition, illness or injury, or be age 19 or younger or age 65 or older.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.ontario.ca/page/get-physiotherapy |title=Get physiotherapy: Get government-funded physiotherapy |website=ontario.ca |date=September 4, 2014 |publisher=Queen's Printer for Ontario |access-date=January 19, 2017}}</ref>

===Other coverage limitations===
Coverage varies for care related to the feet. In Ontario, as of 2019, Medicare covers between $7–16 of each visit to a registered [[podiatrist]] up to $135 per patient per year, plus $30 for x-rays.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.ontario.ca/page/what-ohip-covers |title=What OHIP covers |website=www.ontario.ca |date=April 21, 2017 |access-date=February 19, 2019}}</ref> Although the elderly, as well as diabetic patients, may have needs that greatly exceed that limit, such costs would have to be covered by patients or private supplemental insurance.

As of 2014, most, but not all provinces and territories provide some coverage for sex reassignment surgery (also known as gender confirming surgery) and other treatment for [[gender dysphoria]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Rose|first=Rebecca|date=July 24, 2014|title=Sex-reassignment surgeries funded in all but two provinces - But gaps remain in which surgeries covered where for trans Canadians|url=https://xtramagazine.com/power/sex-reassignment-surgeries-funded-in-all-but-two-provinces-62534|access-date=December 6, 2021|website=Daily Xtra|publisher=Pink Triangle Press}}</ref> In Ontario, sex reassignment surgery requires prior approval before being covered.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.health.gov.on.ca/en/pro/programs/srs/ |title=Sex Reassignment Surgery |website=health.gov.on.ca |publisher=Queen's Printer for Ontario |access-date=January 19, 2017}}</ref>

However, access to care does not meet [[World Professional Association for Transgender Health|WPATH]] guidelines in provinces covering 84% of Canada's population (excepting British Columbia, Prince Edward Island and Yukon Territory). Wait times are extensive for gender care in Canada, and can be as long as eight years.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-08-16 |title=Wait times for bottom surgery in Canada can be as long as eight years. The impact on individuals can be deadly {{!}} Xtra Magazine |url=https://xtramagazine.com/health/wait-times-trans-bottom-surgery-canada-255804 |access-date=2024-03-09 |language=en-CA}}</ref>

There are wide discrepancies in coverage for various assistive devices such as wheelchairs and respiratory equipment in Canada. Ontario, which has one of the most generous programs, pays 75% of the cost for listed equipment and supplies for persons with a disability requiring such equipment or supplies for six months or longer.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.ontario.ca/page/assistive-devices-program |title=Assistive Devices Program |website=ontario.ca |date=December 7, 2016 |publisher=Queen's Printer for Ontario |access-date=January 19, 2017}}</ref> The program does not have age or income restrictions. As with other health coverage, veterans and others covered by federal programs are not eligible under the provincial program. Only certain types of equipment and supplies are covered, and within categories only approved models of equipment from approved vendors are covered, and vendors may not charge more than specified prices established by the government.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.ontario.ca/page/mobility-aids |title=Mobility aids |website=ontario.ca |publisher=Queen's Printer for Ontario |access-date=January 19, 2017}}</ref>

==Indigenous peoples==

The largest group the federal government is directly responsible for is [[First Nations in Canada|First Nations]]. Native peoples are a federal responsibility and the federal government guarantees complete coverage of their health needs. For the last twenty years and despite health care being a guaranteed right for First Nations due to the many treaties the government of Canada signed for access to First Nations lands and resources, the amount of coverage provided by the Federal government's [[Non-Insured Health Benefits]] program has diminished drastically for optometry, dentistry, and medicines. Status First Nations individuals qualify for a set number of visits to the optometrist and dentist, with a limited amount of coverage for glasses, eye exams, fillings, root canals, etc. For the most part, First Nations people use normal hospitals and the federal government then fully compensates the provincial government for the expense. The federal government also covers any user fees the province charges. The federal government maintains a network of clinics and health centers on [[Indian reserve|First Nations reserves]]. At the provincial level, there are also several much smaller health programs alongside Medicare. The largest of these is the health care costs paid by the [[workers' compensation]] system. Regardless of federal efforts, healthcare for First Nations has generally not been considered effective.<ref name="CMAJ_Silversides_2007">{{Cite journal |last=Silversides |first=Ann |date=October 23, 2007 |title=The North "like Darfur" |journal=Canadian Medical Association Journal |volume=177 |issue=9 |pages=1013–4 |doi=10.1503/cmaj.071359 |pmc=2025628 |pmid=17954876}}</ref><ref name="CMAJ_Song_2008">{{Cite journal |last=Gao |first=Song  |date=November 4, 2008 |title=Access to health care among status Aboriginal people with chronic kidney disease |journal=Canadian Medical Association Journal |volume=179 |issue=10 |pages=1007–12 |doi=10.1503/cmaj.080063 |pmc=2572655 |pmid=18981441}}</ref><ref name="CMAJ_Peiris_2008">{{Cite journal |last1=Peiris |first1=David |last2=Alex Brown |last3=BMed MPH |last4=Alan Cass |last5=MBBS PhD |date=November 4, 2008 |title=Addressing inequities in access to quality health care for indigenous people |journal=Canadian Medical Association Journal |volume=179 |issue=10 |pages=985–6 |doi=10.1503/cmaj.081445 |pmc=2572646 |pmid=18981431}}</ref> Despite being a provincial responsibility, the large health costs have long been partially funded by the federal government.

==Healthcare spending==
While the Canadian healthcare system has been called a [[single payer system]], Canada "does not have a single health care system" according to a 2018 Library of Parliament report.<ref name="LoP_Norris_20180718"/> The provinces and territories provide "publicly funded health care" through provincial and territorial public health insurance systems.<ref name="LoP_Norris_20180718"/> The total health expenditure in Canada includes expenditures for those health services not covered by either federal funds or these public insurance systems, that are paid by private insurance or by individuals out-of-pocket.<ref name="LoP_Norris_20180718"/>

In 2017, the [[Canadian Institute for Health Information]] reported that healthcare spending is expected to reach $242 billion, or 11.5% of Canada's [[gross domestic product]] for that year.

The provinces and territories health spending accounted for approximately "64.2% of total health expenditure" in 2018. <ref name="LoP_Norris_20180718" /><ref name="CIHI_Trends_2018" /> Public sources of revenue for the public healthcare system include provincial financing which represented 64.2% of the total in 2018. This includes funds transferred from the federal government to the provinces in the form of the CHT.<ref name="LoP_Norris_20180718" /> Direct funding from the federal government, as well as funds from municipal governments and social security funds represented 4.8% in 2018.<ref name="LoP_Norris_20180718" /><ref name="CIHI_Trends_2018" />{{rp|11}}

According to the CIHI 2019 report, since 1997, the 70–30 split between public and private sector healthcare spending has remained relatively consistent with approximately 70% of Canada's total health expenditures from the public sector and 30% from the private sector.<ref name="CIHI_2019" /><ref name="CIHI_2005">{{Cite book |url=http://www.cihi.ca/cihiweb/dispPage.jsp?cw_page=AR_1282_E |title=CIHI exploring the 70-30 split |last=Canadian Institute for Health Information |date=September 27, 2005 |publisher=Canadian Institute for Health Information |isbn=978-1-55392-655-9 |location=Ottawa, Ont. |author-link=Canadian Institute for Health Information |access-date=December 21, 2007 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20060319000252/http://www.cihi.ca/cihiweb/dispPage.jsp?cw_page=AR_1282_E |archive-date=March 19, 2006 }}</ref> Public-sector funding, which has represented approximately 70% of total health expenditure since 1997, "includes payments by governments at the federal, provincial / territorial and municipal levels and by workers' compensation boards and other social security schemes".<ref name="CIHI_Trends_2018">{{cite report |title=National Health Expenditure Trends 1975 to 2019 |work=[[Canadian Institute for Health Information]] (CIHI) |url=https://www.cihi.ca/en/national-health-expenditure-trends-1975-to-2018 |access-date=January 8, 2021 |date=2019 |page=44 |isbn=978-1-77109-757-4 }}{{Dead link|date=July 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>{{rp|11}}

==Private sector funding==
Private sector funding is regulated under the ''Canada Health Act'', (CHA) which sets the conditions with which provincial / territorial health insurance plans must comply if they wish to receive their full transfer payments from the federal government. The CHA does not allow charges to insured persons for insured services (defined as medically necessary care provided in hospitals or by physicians). Most provinces have responded through various prohibitions on such payments.<ref name="CIHI_2005"/>

Private-sector health care dollars, which has represented about 30% of total health expenditure, "consists primarily of health expenditures by households and private insurance firms".<ref name="CIHI_Trends_2018"/> In 2018, private sector funding for health care, accounted for 31% of the total health expenditures.<ref name="LoP_Norris_20180718"/> "includes primarily private insurance and household expenditures."<ref name="LoP_Norris_20180718"/>

The top categories of private sector expenditures account for 66% of this spending, and include pharmaceuticals, and professional services such as dental and vision care services.<ref name="CIHI_2019"/> Only 10% of these services are paid for by the public sector.<ref name="CIHI_2019"/> In 2017, 41% of private sector expenses were paid by private insurance companies. The amount of out-of-pocket spending represented 49% of private sector spending.<ref name="CIHI_2019"/>

A 2006 in-depth CBC report, the Canadian system is for the most part publicly funded, yet most of the services are provided by private enterprises.<ref name="CBC_2006">{{Cite news| title = CBC News In Depth: Health care| access-date = January 10, 2021| date = December 1, 2006| url = https://www.cbc.ca/news2/background/healthcare/public_vs_private.html}}</ref> In 2006, most doctors do not receive an annual salary, but receive a fee per visit or service.<ref name="CBC_2006"/> According to Dr. Albert Schumacher, former president of the [[Canadian Medical Association]], an "estimated 75% of Canadian health care services are delivered privately but funded publicly."<ref name="CBC_2006"/> 
{{blockquote|"Front line practitioners whether they're GP's or specialists, by and large, are not salaried. They're small hardware stores. Same thing with labs and radiology clinics{{nbsp}}... The situation we are seeing now are more services around not being funded publicly but people having to pay for them, or their insurance companies. We have sort of a passive privatization."| Dr. Albert Schumacher. CBC. December 1, 2006.}}

Private clinics are permitted and are regulated by the provinces and territories. Private clinics can charge above the agreed-upon fee schedule if they are providing non-insured services, treating non-insured persons, or based in Quebec, due to a court decision.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Chaoulli v. Quebec |url=https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/chaoulli-v-quebec |access-date=2024-08-01 |website=www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca |language=en}}</ref> This may include those eligible under automobile insurance or worker's compensation, in addition to those who are not Canadian residents, or providing non-insured services. This provision has been controversial among those seeking a greater role for private funding.

It's been suggested<ref name="Maple">[https://www.theaudit.ca/p/the-canada-health-act-may-already] The Audit, 2024. Retrieved February 7, 2024.</ref> that the apparent success of the private telehealth provider Maple, with its hundreds of thousands of paying users, indicates the existence of a rapidly growing private healthcare tier. Maple has come under criticism for affordability,<ref>{{Cite news |last=Lupton |first=Andrew |date=July 10, 2017 |title=Controversial for-fee service connects Ontario doctors and patients via video chat |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/london/maple-health-online-doctor-visits-1.4194285 |work=CBC News}}</ref> as appointments with a general practitioner on Maple can cost over $200 per visit.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Pricing in Quebec |url=https://www.getmaple.ca/pricing-quebec/ |access-date=2024-08-01 |website=Maple |language=en-US}}</ref>

===Private health insurance===
In Canada private health insurances is mainly provided through employers.<ref name="OECD_health_project_2004"/>

By 2016, "health care dollars from private insurance were $788 per capita" in 2016, which represents an annual growth rate of 6.4% from 1988 to 2016.<ref name="LoP_Norris_20180718"/>

According to a 2004 OECD report, 75% of Canadians had some form of supplementary private health insurance.<ref name="OECD_health_project_2004">[https://books.google.com/books?id=oUM39nDp2s4C&q=employer+provided+private+health+insurance+in+canada Private Health Insurance in OECD Countries] OECD Health Project, 2004. Retrieved January 21, 2008.</ref>

In many provinces, purchasing duplicate health insurance for care already covered by the government's health insurance plan is prohibited.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Real Solutions for What Ails Canada's Health Care Systems – Lessons from Sweden and the United Kingdom {{!}} Montreal Economic Institute |url=https://www.iedm.org/real-solutions-for-what-ails-canadas-health-care-systems-lessons-from-sweden-and-the-united-kingdom/ |access-date=2023-01-27 |website=www.iedm.org |date=February 17, 2022 |language=en-US}}</ref>{{verify source|date=January 2023}}

===Out-of-pocket expenses===
From 1988 to 2016, the amount of out‑of‑pocket expenses paid by individuals had grown by about 4.6% annually. By 2016, it amounted to $972 per capita.<ref name="LoP_Norris_20180718"/>

===Major healthcare expenses===
The highest health expenditures were hospitals—$51B in 2009 up from $45.4B, representing 28.2% in 2007, followed by [[medication|pharmaceuticals]]—$30B in 2009 up from $26.5B, representing 16.5% in 2007, and physician services—$26B in 2009, up from $21.5B or 13.4% in 2007.<ref name="CBC2009">{{Cite news |url=http://www.cbc.ca/news/technology/canadian-health-care-spending-to-top-180b-1.862565 |title=Canadian health-care spending to top $180B |date=November 19, 2009 |work=CBC News |access-date=January 3, 2015}}</ref><ref name="auto">CIHI p.112-113</ref>

The proportion spent on hospitals and physicians has declined between 1975 and 2009 while the amount spent on pharmaceuticals has increased.<ref name="auto2">CIHI p.20</ref> Of the three biggest health care expenses, the amount spent on pharmaceuticals has increased the most. In 1997, the total price of drugs surpassed that of doctors. In 1975, the three biggest health costs were hospitals ($5.5B / 44.7%), physicians ($1.8B / 15.1%), and medications ($1.1B / 8.8%).<ref name="auto"/>

By 2018, drugs (both prescription and non-prescription) had become the second largest expenditure representing 15.3% of the total, hospitals at 26.6% represented the largest sector by expenses, and physician services represented 15.1% of the total.<ref name="CIHI_Trends_2019"/>

====Hospitals====
Hospitals have consistently been the top healthcare expenditure representing 26.6% of total healthcare expenditures in Canada in 2018.<ref name="CIHI_Trends_2019"/>

Hospital capacity in Canada peaked in 1970. Since then, per-capita hospital bed capacity has been reduced by 63%.<ref name="World Bank Open Data">{{Cite web |title=World Bank Open Data |url=https://data.worldbank.org/ |access-date=2024-08-01 |website=World Bank Open Data}}</ref>

Hospital care is delivered by publicly funded hospitals in Canada. Most of the public hospitals, each of which are independent institutions incorporated under provincial Corporations Acts, are required by law to operate within their budget.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.health.gov.on.ca/english/public/contact/hosp/hospfaq_dt.html |title=Public Information - Public - Hospitals - Questions and Answers - Details |date=July 26, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100726045132/http://www.health.gov.on.ca/english/public/contact/hosp/hospfaq_dt.html |publisher=Ontario Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care |archive-date=July 26, 2010}}</ref> Amalgamation of hospitals in the 1990s has reduced competition between hospitals.

An [[OECD]] study in 2010 noted that there were variations in care across the different provinces in Canada. The study found that there was a difference in hospital admission rates depending on the number of people and what province they lived in. Typically, provinces with low population counts had higher hospital admission rates due to there being a lack of doctors and hospitals in the region.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Alari |first1=A. |first2=G. |last2=Lafortune |first3=D. |last3=Srivastava |name-list-style=amp |date=2014 |title=Canada: Geographic variations in health care |journal=Geographic Variations in Health Care: What do We Know and What Can be Done to Improve Health System Performance? |series=OECD Health Policy Studies |pages=137–169 |publisher=OECD Publishing |location=Paris |doi=10.1787/9789264216594-7-en|isbn=978-92-64-21658-7 }}</ref>

====Pharmaceuticals====
By 2018, drugs—both prescription and non-prescription—were the second largest healthcare expenditure in Canada at 15.3% of the total.<ref name="CIHI_Trends_2019"/>

According to the December 2020 CIHI report, in 2019 public drug programs expenditures were $15 billion, representing a one-year increase of 3%.<ref name="CIHI_prescribeddrugs_20201217">{{Cite report| title = Prescribed drug spending in Canada, 2020| work = CIHI| date = December 17, 2020| access-date = January 10, 2021| url = https://www.cihi.ca/en/prescribed-drug-spending-in-canada-2020| archive-date = January 12, 2021| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210112060350/https://www.cihi.ca/en/prescribed-drug-spending-in-canada-2020}}</ref> The drug that contributed to about 26% of the increase in spending were drugs for diabetes.<ref name="CIHI_prescribeddrugs_20201217"/> In 2018, [[hepatitis C]] drugs were the 2nd highest contributor to increase in pharmaceutical spending. In 2019, this decreased by 18% as fewer people took these drugs. In 2019, spending on [[biologics]] increased from 9% to 17% of public spending for treatment of [[rheumatoid arthritis]], Crohn's disease and similar conditions.<ref name="CIHI_prescribeddrugs_20201217"/>

By 1997, the total cost of pharmaceuticals surpassed the total cost of physician services and has remained in second place, after hospitals in terms of total annual health expenditures.<ref name="auto2"/> The proportion spent on hospitals and physicians has declined between 1975 and 2009 while the amount spent on pharmaceuticals has increased.<ref name="auto2"/> Of the three biggest health care expenses, the amount spent on pharmaceuticals has increased the most. In 1997, the total price of drugs surpassed that of doctors. In 1975, the three biggest health costs were hospitals ($5.5B / 44.7%), physicians ($1.8B / 15.1%), and medications ($1.1B / 8.8%).<ref name="auto"/>

According to the April 2018 report entitled ''Pharmacare Now: Prescription Medicine Coverage for All Canadians'' issued by the House of Commons Standing Committee on Health "spending on medicines dispensed outside hospitals accounted for 85% of total drug expenditures in 2017."<ref name="LoP_Norris_20180718">{{Cite conference| publisher = Library of Parliament| page = 8| last = Norris| first = Sonya| title = Federal Funding for Health Care| location = Ottawa, Ontario| access-date = 2021-01-10| date = 2018-07-18| url = https://lop.parl.ca/sites/PublicWebsite/default/en_CA/ResearchPublications/201845E}}</ref>

The CHA requires that public provincial and territorial health insurance policies must cover all "medicines used within the hospital setting...out‑of‑hospital drug expenditures are paid for by private insurance and individuals, as well as by provincial health insurance for certain population groups".<ref name="LoP_Norris_20180718"/> Public provincial and territorial health insurance covers "43% of out‑of‑hospital medicine"; private insurance covers 35%; and the remainder, which represents 22% is paid by individuals out-of-pocket.<ref name="LoP_Norris_20180718"/>

Pharmaceutical costs are set at a global median by the government [[price controls]].

====Physician services====
The third largest healthcare expenditure in Canada are physician services which represented 15.1% of the total in 2018.<ref name="CIHI_Trends_2019"/> From 1997 through 2009, the proportion of total annual health expenditures spent on physicians declined.<ref name="auto2"/>

In 2007, physician services cost $21.5B representing 13.4% of total health expenditures.<ref name="CBC2009"/> By 2009, that had increased to $26B.<ref name="CBC2009"/>

Canada, like its North American neighbor the United States, has a ratio of practising physicians to a population that is below the OECD average<ref name="number of docs">[https://data.oecd.org/healthres/doctors.htm Health resources - Doctors]. [[OECD]] Data.</ref> but a level of practising nurses that is higher than the OECD average, though below the US average in 2016.<ref name="numberofnurses">[https://data.oecd.org/healthres/nurses.htm#indicator-chart Health resources - Nurses]. OECD Data.</ref>

A record number of doctors was reported in 2012 with 75,142 physicians, though this includes doctors who have partially or completely opted out of the public health system, which has occurred at record numbers in Quebec.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Derfel |first=Aaron |date=July 29, 2024 |title=780 doctors opted out of medicare in Quebec. Only 14 have in the rest of Canada |url=https://montrealgazette.com/news/local-news/780-doctors-opted-out-of-medicare-in-quebec-only-14-have-in-the-rest-of-canada |access-date=August 1, 2024 |work=The Montreal Gazette}}</ref> The [[Gross (economics)|gross]] average salary was $328,000. Out of the gross amount, doctors pay for taxes, rent, staff salaries and equipment.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.cbc.ca/news/health/canadian-doctor-total-at-record-high-1.1869346 |title=Canadian doctor total at record high |access-date=September 28, 2013 |publisher=[[CBC.ca]]}}</ref> Recent reports indicate that Canada has an imbalanced supply of specialists to general physicians, and a severe shortage of family doctors, with 10 million Canadians projected to lack access to primary care,<ref>{{Cite news |last=Kirkey |first=Shannon |date=February 16, 2024 |title=Canada's family doctor shortage: 10 million will soon lack access to primary care |url=https://nationalpost.com/health/canada-family-doctor-shortage |access-date=August 1, 2024 |work=The National Post}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Webster |first=Paul |date=May 17, 2024 |title=Canada's family physician shortage |url=https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(24)01036-5/abstract |journal=The Lancet|volume=403 |issue=10441 |page=2278 |doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(24)01036-5 |pmid=38768629 |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Tasker |first=John Paul |date=February 18, 2024 |title=Meet some of the 6 million Canadians who don't have a family doctor |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/meet-the-canadians-without-a-family-doctor-1.7116475 |access-date=August 1, 2024 |work=CBC News}}</ref> compounded by new graduates opting against selecting family medicine,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Can new approaches to medical curriculum solve the family doctor shortage? |url=https://universityaffairs.ca/features/feature-article/can-new-approaches-to-medical-curriculum-solve-the-family-doctor-shortage/ |access-date=2024-08-01 |website=University Affairs |date=March 20, 2024 |language=en-US}}</ref> and communities in rural, remote and northern regions, experience particularly acute shortages.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://umanitoba.ca/outreach/evidencenetwork/archives/15205 |title=More health specialists not the answer to health system woes |website=Umanitoba.ca |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141220021732/http://umanitoba.ca/outreach/evidencenetwork/archives/15205 |archive-date=December 20, 2014 |access-date=September 19, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://nationalpost.com/opinion/maria-mathews-calling-all-country-doctors |title=Maria Mathews: Calling all country doctors |date=February 22, 2013 |website=Nationalpost.ca}}</ref> Limitations on which and how many physicians can complete Canada's required two year medical residency may prevent trained doctors from acquiring a license to practice medicine, leading to an effective shortage.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/canada-turning-away-home-grown-doctors-1.6743486 |title=Canada is short of doctors — and it's turning away hundreds of its own physicians each year | date=February 10, 2023 |website=cbc.ca |access-date=April 13, 2023}}</ref> Burnout and mental health reasons may also play a role, as in 2021, 48% of physicians polled by the Canadian Medical Association screened positive for depression.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Nassar |first=Hana Mae |date=2022-08-25 |title=Canadian doctors struggle amid pressures |url=https://vancouver.citynews.ca/2022/08/25/canadian-doctor-despair-staffing-pressures/ |access-date=2024-08-01 |website=CityNews Vancouver}}</ref>

=====Physician payment=====
Basic services are provided by private doctors (since 2002 they have been allowed to incorporate), with the entire fee paid for by the government at the same rate. 
Most family doctors receive a fee per visit. These rates are negotiated between the provincial governments and the province's medical associations, usually on an annual basis. The fee for service model has been criticized for deterring physicians from becoming family doctors in British Columbia.<ref>{{Cite news |date=November 12, 2021 |title=Fee-for-service model is deterring aspiring family doctors from setting up practice: report |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/fee-for-service-model-family-doctors-1.6247049 |access-date=August 1, 2024 |work=CBC News}}</ref>

CTV news reported that, in 2006, family physicians in Canada made an average of $202,000 a year.<ref name="CTV.ca">{{Cite web |url=http://www.ctv.ca/servlet/ArticleNews/story/CTVNews/20061221/quebec_doctors_061221?s_name=&no_ads= |title=Que. doctors lagging in fee-for-service payments |date=December 21, 2006 |publisher=Ctv.ca |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090610013445/http://www.ctv.ca/servlet/ArticleNews/story/CTVNews/20061221/quebec_doctors_061221?s_name=&no_ads= |archive-date=June 10, 2009 |access-date=February 10, 2011}}</ref>

In 2018, to draw attention to the low pay of nurses and the declining level of service provided to patients, more than 700 physicians, residents and medical students in Quebec signed an [[online petition]] asking for their pay raises to be canceled.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/worldviews/wp/2018/03/07/hundreds-of-canadian-doctors-demand-lower-salaries/ |title=Hundreds of Canadian doctors demand lower salaries. (Yes, lower.) |last=Wang |first=Amy |date=March 7, 2018 |work=washingtonpost.com}}</ref>

=====Professional organizations=====
Each province regulates its medical profession through a self-governing [[Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada|College of Physicians and Surgeons]], which is responsible for licensing physicians, setting practice standards, and investigating and disciplining its members.

The national doctors association is called the [[Canadian Medical Association]] (CMA);<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.cma.ca/index.cfm/ci_id/121/la_id/1.htm |title=Canadian Medical Association |publisher=Cma.ca |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090708163655/http://www.cma.ca/index.cfm/ci_id/121/la_id/1.htm |archive-date=July 8, 2009 |access-date=February 10, 2011}}</ref> it describes its mission as "To serve and unite the physicians of Canada and be the national advocate, in partnership with the people of Canada, for the highest standards of health and health care."<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.cma.ca/index.cfm/ci_id/44413/la_id/1.htm |title=About CMA |date=March 24, 2010 |publisher=Cma.ca |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060502120835/http://www.cma.ca/index.cfm/ci_id/44413/la_id/1.htm |archive-date=May 2, 2006 |access-date=February 10, 2011}}</ref>

Since the passage of the 1984 ''Canada Health Act'', the CMA itself has been a strong advocate of maintaining a strong publicly funded system, including lobbying the federal government to increase funding, and being a founding member of (and active participant in) the Health Action Lobby (HEAL).<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.physiotherapy.ca/HEAL/english/index.htm |title=HEAL home page |publisher=Physiotherapy.ca |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110310065556/http://www.physiotherapy.ca/heal/english/index.htm |archive-date=March 10, 2011 |access-date=February 10, 2011}}</ref>

In December 2008, the [[Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada]] reported a critical shortage of [[obstetricians]] and [[gynaecologists|gynecologists]]. The report stated that 1,370 obstetricians were practising in Canada and that number is expected to fall by at least one-third within five years. The society is asking the government to increase the number of [[medical school]] spots for obstetrics and gynecologists by 30 percent a year for three years and also recommended rotating placements of doctors into smaller communities to encourage them to take up residence there.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.ctvnews.ca/obstetrician-shortage-endangers-moms-babies-report-1.349079 |title=Obstetrician shortage endangers moms, babies: report says |date=December 5, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081206233508/http://www.ctv.ca/servlet/ArticleNews/story/CTVNews/20081205/ob_shortage_081205/20081205?hub=Health |archive-date=December 6, 2008 |publisher=[[CTV.ca]]}}</ref>

Some provincial medical associations have argued for permitting a larger private role. To some extent, this has been a reaction to strong cost control; CIHI estimates that 99% of physician expenditures in Canada come from public sector sources, and physicians—particularly those providing elective procedures who have been squeezed for operating room time—have accordingly looked for alternative revenue sources. The CMA presidency rotates among the provinces, with the provincial association electing a candidate who is customarily ratified by the CMA general meeting. Day's selection was sufficiently controversial that he was challenged—albeit unsuccessfully—by another physician.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/prince-edward-island/private-health-care-advocate-wins-cma-presidency-1.588876|title=CBC Private health-care advocate wins CMA presidency |date=August 22, 2006 |access-date=February 10, 2011 |publisher=CBC.ca}}</ref>

Because healthcare is deemed to be under provincial / territorial jurisdiction, negotiations on behalf of physicians are conducted by provincial associations such as the Ontario Medical Association. The views of Canadian doctors have been mixed, particularly in their support for allowing parallel private financing. The history of Canadian physicians in the development of Medicare has been described by C. [[David Naylor]].<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/privatepracticep0000nayl_w9u4 |title=Private Practice, Public Payment: Canadian Medicine and the Politics of Health Insurance 1911-1966 |last=Naylor |first=C David |publisher=McGill-Queen's University Press |year=1986 |location=Kingston, Ontario |isbn=978-0-7735-6111-3 |url-access=registration}}</ref>
