===Healthcare spending and an aging population===
By 2019, Canada's aging population represented a modest increase in healthcare costs of about 1% a year.<ref name="CIHI_2019"/> It is also the greatest at the extremes of age at a cost of $17,469 per capita in those older than 80 and $8,239 for those less than 1 year old in comparison to $3,809 for those between 1 and 64 years old in 2007.<ref name="CIHI p.xiv"/>

===Comparing healthcare spending over time===

Healthcare spending in Canada (in 1997 dollars) has increased each year between 1975 and 2009, from $39.7 billion to $137.3 billion, or per capita spending from $1,715 to $4089.<ref>CIHI pg. 119</ref> In 2013 the total reached $211 billion, averaging $5,988 per person.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.cihi.ca/en/nhex_infosheet_2013_en.pdf |title=Health Spending in 2013 |website=Cihi.ca |access-date=May 27, 2018 |archive-date=March 4, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304041959/https://www.cihi.ca/en/nhex_infosheet_2013_en.pdf }}</ref> Figures in National Health Expenditure Trends, 1975 to 2012, show that the pace of growth is slowing. Modest economic growth and budgetary deficits are having a moderating effect. For the third straight year, growth in healthcare spending will be less than that in the overall economy. The proportion of Canada's gross domestic product will reach 11.6% in 2012 down from 11.7% in 2011 and the all-time high of 11.9% in 2010.<ref>[http://www.cihi.ca/cihi-ext-portal/internet/en/document/spending+and+health+workforce/spending/release_30oct12 Canada's health care spending growth slows] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130615125013/http://www.cihi.ca/CIHI-ext-portal/internet/en/Document/spending+and+health+workforce/spending/RELEASE_30OCT12 |date=June 15, 2013 }}. Canadian Institute for Health Information (CIHI). Retrieved: May 28, 2013.</ref> Total spending in 2007 was equivalent to 10.1% of the gross domestic product which was slightly above the average for OECD countries, and below the 16.0% of GDP spent in the United States.<ref>CIHI p.55</ref>

Since 1999, 70% of Canada's total health expenditures is from the public sector and 30% from the private sector.<ref name="CIHI_2019"/><ref name="CIHI_2005"/> This was slightly below the OECD average of public health spending in 2009.<ref name="CIHI p.xiii">CIHI p.xiii</ref> Public sector funding included most hospital and physician costs with the other 30% primarily paid by individuals through their private or workplace insurance or out-of-pocket.<ref>CIHI p. xiii"</ref> Half of private health expenditure comes from private insurance and the remaining half is supplied by out-of-pocket payments.<ref name="CIHI_2019"/><ref name="CIHI_2005"/>

There is considerable variation across the provinces / territories as to the extent to which such costs as out of hospital prescription medications, assistive devices, physical therapy, long-term care, dental care and [[Emergency medical services in Canada|ambulance services]] are covered.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.health.gov.on.ca/en/public/publications/ohip/amb.aspx|title=Ambulance Services Billing - Ontario Health Insurance (OHIP) - Publications - Public Information - MOHLTC|first=Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care|last=Government of Ontario|website=www.health.gov.on.ca}}</ref>

===Healthcare spending by province===
The planning and funding of most publicly insured health services are the responsibility of provinces and territories. There is a regional variation in health system characteristics.

Healthcare costs per capita vary across Canada with Quebec ($4,891) and British Columbia ($5,254) at the lowest level and Alberta ($6,072) and Newfoundland ($5,970) at the highest.<ref name="CIHI p.xiv"/>

Total health spending per resident varies from $7,378 in Newfoundland and Labrador to $6,321 in British Columbia. Public drug spending increased by 4.5% in 2016, driven largely by prescriptions for [[tumor necrosis factor alpha]] and [[hepatitis C]] drugs.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.cihi.ca/en/total-health-spending-in-canada-reaches-242-billion |title=Total health spending in Canada reaches $242 billion |date=November 7, 2017 |website=Canadian Institute for Health Information |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190421231735/https://www.cihi.ca/en/total-health-spending-in-canada-reaches-242-billion |archive-date=April 21, 2019 |access-date=November 8, 2017 |quote=Spending on drugs is expected to outpace spending on hospitals and doctors.}}</ref>

According to a 2003 article by Lightman, "In-kind delivery in Canada is superior to the American market approach in its efficiency of delivery." In the US, 13.6 percent of [[GNP]] is used in medical care. By contrast, in Canada, only 9.5 percent of GNP is used on the Medicare system, "in part because there is no profit incentive for private insurers." Lightman also notes that the in-kind delivery system eliminates much of the advertising that is prominent in the US and the low overall administrative costs in the in-kind delivery system. Since there are no means tests and no bad-debt problems for doctors under the Canadian in-kind system, doctors billing and collection costs are reduced to almost zero.<ref>Ernie Lightman, 2003 Social policy in Canada Toronto: Oxford University Press pg 130-131</ref>

==A timeline of significant events in Canadian healthcare==
{{Main|History of medicine in Canada}}

The ''[[Constitution Act, 1867]]'' (formerly called the ''British North America Act, 1867'') did not give either the federal or provincial governments responsibility for healthcare, as it was then a minor concern. However, the Act did give the provinces responsibility for regulating hospitals, and the provinces claimed that their general responsibility for local and private matters encompassed healthcare. The federal government felt that the health of the population fell under the "[[Peace, order, and good government]]" part of its responsibilities.{{citation needed|date=November 2021}}

The [[Judicial Committee of the Privy Council]] ruled that the federal government had the responsibility of protecting the health and well-being of the population,{{citation needed|date=November 2021}} and that the provinces had the responsibility of administering and delivering healthcare.

Before 1966, [[Veterans Affairs Canada]] had a large healthcare network, but this was merged into the general system with the creation of Medicare.

In 1975, Health Canada, which was then known as National Health and Welfare, established the National Health Research and Development Program.

In 1977, cost-sharing agreement between the federal and provincial governments, through the ''[[Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act]]'' and extended by the ''Medical Care Act'' was discontinued. It was replaced by [[Established Programs Financing]]. This gave a bloc transfer to the provinces, giving them more flexibility but also reducing the federal influence on the health system. Almost all government health spending goes through Medicare, but there are several smaller programs.

Provinces developed their own programs, for example, [[OHIP]] in [[Ontario]], that are required to meet the general guidelines laid out in the federal ''Canada Health Act''. The federal government directly administers health to groups such as the military, and inmates of federal prisons. They also provide some care to the [[Royal Canadian Mounted Police]] and veterans, but these groups mostly use the public system.

In 1996, when faced with a large budget shortfall, the Liberal federal government merged the health transfers with the transfers for other social programs into the [[Canada Health and Social Transfer]], and overall funding levels were cut. This placed considerable pressure on the provinces and combined with [[population aging]] and the generally high rate of [[inflation]] in health costs, has caused problems with the system.

The 2002 [[Royal Commission on the Future of Health Care in Canada]], also known as the Romanow Report, was published.<ref name="Romanow_Report_2002"/>

The Canadian Health Coalition formed in 2002.<ref name="Romanow_Report_2002"/>

In 2004, the First Ministers came to an agreement with the federal government on a ten-year plan to improve Canada's healthcare.<ref name="HC_FirstMinisters_2004">{{Cite conference| title = A 10-year plan to strengthen health care - 2004 First Ministers' Meeting on the Future of Health Care| date = 2004| url = http://www.hc-sc.gc.ca/hcs-sss/delivery-prestation/fptcollab/2004-fmm-rpm/index-eng.php| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110819164453/http://www.hc-sc.gc.ca/hcs-sss/delivery-prestation/fptcollab/2004-fmm-rpm/index-eng.php |archive-date=August 19, 2011}}</ref> Areas of focus included wait times, home care, primary care reform, national pharmaceuticals strategy, prevention, promotion and public health, aboriginal health, and the First Nations and Inuit Health Branch (FNIHB) at Health Canada.<ref name="HC_FirstMinisters_2004"/>

In 2006, [[Stephen Harper]] won the federal election on a "platform that pushed for a mix of public and private health care, provided that health care stays publicly funded and universally accessible".<ref name="CBC_2006"/>

==Healthcare debates in Canada==

==Flaws in Canada's healthcare system==
Identified weaknesses of Canada's system were comparatively higher infant mortality rate, the prevalence of chronic conditions, long wait times, poor availability of after-hours care, and a lack of prescription drugs coverage.<ref name="Prescription for Canada"/> Limited dental coverage was added in 2023.<ref name="Reason magazine, September 7th, 2022">{{cite web |last1=Shackford |first1=Scott |title=Some Canadian Health Care Patients Say They're Being Encouraged To Just Die Already |url=https://reason.com/2022/09/07/some-canadian-health-care-patients-say-theyre-being-encouraged-to-just-die-already/ |website=reason.com |date=September 7, 2022 |publisher=Reason |access-date=8 September 2022}}</ref><ref name="auto3"/> An increasing problem in Canada's health system is a shortage of healthcare professionals and hospital capacity.<ref name="Duong Vogel 2023 pp. E309–E310"/>

A 2016 study by the [[Commonwealth Fund]], based in the US, found that Canada's wait time for all categories of services ranked either at the bottom or second to the bottom of the 11 surveyed countries (Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Sweden, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, and the United States). Canada's wait time on emergency services was the longest of the 11 nations, with 29% of Canadians reporting that they waited for more than four hours the last time they went to an emergency department. ===Gender gaps in healthcare===
[[File:Life expectancy by WBG -Canada -diff.png|thumb|upright=1.05|[[Life expectancy]] in Canada by gender]]
Gender gaps in healthcare are significantly influenced by socioeconomic status, geographical location, and ethnicity.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Canada |first=Health |date=2008-01-08 |title=ARCHIVED - Measuring Health Inequalities Among Canadian Women: Developing a Basket of Indicators |url=https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/science-research/reports-publications/health-policy-research/measuring-health-inequalities-among-canadian-women-developing-basket-indicators.html |access-date=2021-12-06 |website=www.canada.ca}}</ref> It has been hypothesized that women experience a higher rate of health-related issues because of their reduced access to the material and social conditions of life that foster good health, as well as a heightened level of stress associated with their gender and marital roles.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Denton |first1=Margaret |last2=Prus |first2=Steven |last3=Walters |first3=Vivienne |date=June 2004 |title=Gender differences in health: a Canadian study of the psychosocial, structural and behavioural determinants of health |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0277953603004726 |journal=Social Science & Medicine |language=en |volume=58 |issue=12 |pages=2585–2600 |doi=10.1016/j.socscimed.2003.09.008|pmid=15081207 }}</ref> Moreover, research has shown that women with low income and who work full-time outside of the house have poorer health status in comparison to their male counterparts.<ref name=":52">{{Cite web |title=Off-Campus Access: Login to e-Resources - McMaster Libraries |url=https://libraryssl.lib.mcmaster.ca/libaccess/login.php?url=https%3a%2f%2fwww.sciencedirect.com%2fscience%2farticle%2fpii%2fS0168851008002388 |access-date=2021-12-06 |website=libraryssl.lib.mcmaster.ca}}</ref>{{Citation needed|date=February 2024}} The added responsibilities women hold as primary caregivers in households not only creates additional stress, but also indirectly increases the difficulty of the scheduling and meeting of medical appointments; these implications explain women's poorer self-rated health status in comparison to men, as well as their report of their unmet healthcare needs.<ref name=":52" />{{Citation needed|date=February 2024}}

Women's additional healthcare requirements, such as pregnancy, further exacerbate the gender gap. Despite comprising approximately half of Canada's population, women receive the majority of Canadian healthcare.<ref name=":02" />

Men and women also experience different wait times for diagnostic tests; longer wait times have been associated with a higher risk of health complications. One Canadian study reports, "mean wait times are significantly lower for men than for women pertaining to overall diagnostic tests: for [[Magnetic resonance imaging|MRI]], 70.3 days for women compared to 29.1 days for men."<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kazanjian |first1=Arminée |last2=Morettin |first2=Denise |last3=Cho |first3=Robert |date=August 25, 2004 |title=Health Care Utilization by Canadian Women |journal=BMC Women's Health |volume=4 |issue=Suppl 1 |pages=S33 |doi=10.1186/1472-6874-4-S1-S33 |pmc=2096683 |pmid=15345096 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

==== Effects of healthcare privatization ====
Disparities between men and women's access to healthcare in Canada have led to criticism, especially regarding healthcare privatization. While most healthcare expenses remain covered by Medicare, certain medical services previously paid for publicly have been shifted to individuals and employer-based supplemental insurance. While this shift has affected both genders, women have been more affected. Compared to men, women are generally less financially stable, and individual payments are a greater burden.<ref name=":02">{{Cite web |url=http://www.womenandhealthcarereform.ca/publications/womenPrivateHealthInsur_en.pdf |title=Women and Private Health Insurance |website=Womenandhealthcarereform.ca |access-date=May 27, 2018}}</ref> Furthermore, many women work part-time or in fields that do not offer supplemental insurance, such as [[homemaking]]. As such, women are less likely to have private insurance to cover the costs of drugs and healthcare services.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/corporate/about-health-canada/reports-publications/women-health-strategy.html#gender |title=Women's Health Strategy |last1=Canada |first1=Health |date=April 22, 2005 |website=aem |access-date=May 4, 2018}}</ref>

The shift from public to private financing has also meant additional labor for women due to families relying on them as caregivers. Less public financing has shifted care to women, leaving "them with more support to provide at home."<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.cwhn.ca/en/node/39564 |title=Health Care Privatization: Women Are Paying the Price {{!}} Canadian Women's Health Network |website=Cwhn.ca |access-date=May 4, 2018}}</ref>

Women's additional healthcare requirements, such as pregnancy, further exacerbate the gender gap. Despite comprising approximately half of Canada's population, women receive the majority of Canadian healthcare.<ref name=":02" />

==== Indigenous community ====
It is well documented in the literature that [[Indigenous peoples in Canada]] lack equitable access to healthcare services for a variety of reasons.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bourassa |first=Carrie |date=January 2018 |title=Addressing the Duality of Access to Healthcare for Indigenous Communities: Racism and Geographical Barriers to Safe Care |journal=HealthcarePapers |volume=17 |issue=3 |pages=6–10 |doi=10.12927/hcpap.2018.25507 |issn=1929-6339 |pmid=30052180}}</ref> One major reason for this inequitable access is due to Indigenous locations of residence. Statistics Canada reported that the majority of Métis live in urban centres, while almost half of First Nations people live on reserves.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Government of Canada |first=Statistics Canada |date=2017-10-25 |title=The Daily — Aboriginal peoples in Canada: Key results from the 2016 Census |url=https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/daily-quotidien/171025/dq171025a-eng.htm |access-date=2021-11-26 |website=www150.statcan.gc.ca}}</ref> In rural northern communities, they struggle to attract and retain healthcare professionals, leaving a great shortage in services that results in far lesser access to care.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Huot |first1=S. |last2=Ho |first2=H. |last3=Ko |first3=A. |last4=Lam |first4=S. |last5=Tactay |first5=P. |last6=MacLachlan |first6=J. |last7=Raanaas |first7=R. One study examined an Inuit community in Rigolet, Canada, and looked at the direct and indirect costs of these long-distance healthcare visits, including missed paid employment, mental well-being costs, transportation costs and others. Altogether, this community experiences healthcare costs greater than other Canadian non-Indigenous and urban areas.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=King |first1=Nia |last2=Vriezen |first2=Rachael |last3=Edge |first3=Victoria L. |last4=Ford |first4=James |last5=Wood |first5=Michele |last6=Team |first6=IHACC Research |last7=Government |first7=Rigolet Inuit Community |last8=Harper |first8=Sherilee |date=2018-05-16 |title=The hidden costs: Identification of indirect costs associated with acute gastrointestinal illness in an Inuit community |journal=PLOS ONE |language=en |volume=13 |issue=5 |article-number=e0196990 |bibcode=2018PLoSO..1396990K |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0196990 |issn=1932-6203 |pmc=5955559 |pmid=29768456 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Another prominent reason for inequitable access to care is the persistence of racism that remains in Canada.<ref name=":22">{{Cite web |last=Government of Canada |first=Public Services and Procurement Canada |date=2002-07-01 |title=Empathy, dignity, and respect : creating cultural safety for Aboriginal people in urban health care: H174-39/2012E-PDF - Government of Canada Publications - Canada.ca |url=https://publications.gc.ca/site/eng/9.698021/publication.html |access-date=2021-11-26 |website=publications.gc.ca}}</ref> In 2012, The Health Council of Canada conducted a series of meetings across the country with a variety of healthcare workers, researchers and Aboriginal people. Through their conversations, they discovered that a large part of the problem comes from the healthcare system. They found that many Indigenous people simply do not trust mainstream health service due to stereotyping, racism and that they feel intimidated. One participant described their experiences as "being treated with contempt, judged, ignored, stereotyped, racialized, and minimized." Finally the Health Council of Canada went on to describe that this lack of equitable access comes as an extension of systemic racism in Canada.<ref name=":22" />

A 2015 study examined 80 Indigenous women who experienced neurological conditions.<ref name=":32">{{Cite journal |last1=Bourassa |first1=Carrie |last2=Blind |first2=Melissa |last3=Dietrich |first3=Devin |last4=Oleson |first4=Eric |date=2015-12-17 |title=Understanding the intergenerational effects of colonization: Aboriginal women with neurological conditions—their reality and resilience |journal=International Journal of Indigenous Health |language=en |volume=10 |issue=2 |pages=3–20 |doi=10.18357/ijih.102201515113 |issn=2291-9376 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Participants described their lack of access to health services to stem from the racism and sexism experienced in the system. They described how important it is for the health system to implement culturally safe care. They also discussed how many stereotyping problems occur in medical school and that Canada requires further Indigenous-centred training. They recommend higher education and awareness training amongst medical schools and healthcare institutions to address the growing healthcare disparities between Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples in Canada.<ref name=":32" />

Canadian Indigenous women face significant disparities in cervical cancer prevention and screening. ==== LGBT community ====
Canadians in the [[LGBT in Canada|LGBT community]], especially those in poverty, receive inadequate levels of treatment. A research study by Lori Ross and Margaret Gibson notes that of all demographics, LGBT members need mental health services the most due to systemic discrimination. According to the study, LGBT members often need to turn to mental health services that are mainly private and not covered by publicly funded healthcare. Low-income LGBT members might be unable to afford these private programs; subsequently, their mental health issues may remain unaddressed or even worsen.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ross |first1=Lori E. |last2=Gibson |first2=Margaret F. |last3=Daley |first3=Andrea |last4=Steele |first4=Leah S. |last5=Williams |first5=Charmaine C. |date=August 14, 2018 |title=In spite of the system: A qualitatively-driven mixed-methods analysis of the mental health services experiences of LGBTQ people living in poverty in Ontario, Canada |journal=PLOS ONE |volume=13 |issue=8 |article-number=e0201437 |bibcode=2018PLoSO..1301437R |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0201437 |pmc=6093609 |pmid=30110350|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Researcher Emily Colpitts states that LGBT members in [[Nova Scotia]] experience ambiguous or alienating language in their health policies. According to Colpitts, the "heteronormative and [[Gender binary|gender-binary language]] and structure of medical intake forms have the consequence of alienating LGBT populations." Colpitts adds that in the previous study of queer and transgender women in Nova Scotia, patients experienced significant discomfort in their meetings with healthcare providers and feared that because of the language of health policy, they would not be able to receive adequate healthcare based on their [[Sexual identity|sexual identities]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Colpitts |first1=Emily |last2=Gahagan |first2=Jacqueline |date=September 22, 2016 |title="I feel like I am surviving the health care system": understanding LGBTQ health in Nova Scotia, Canada |journal=BMC Public Health |volume=16 |issue=1 |page=1005 |doi=10.1186/s12889-016-3675-8 |pmc=5034675 |pmid=27658489 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

According to researcher Judith MacDonnell, LGBT members, especially childbearing lesbians, have trouble navigating through health policy. MacDonnell states that LGBT women encounter challenges at every point of the childbearing process in Canada and have to rely on personal and professional means to receive information that they can understand, such as in reproductive health clinics and postpartum or parenting support.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=MacDonnell |first=Judith A. |title=LGBT Health Care Access: Considering the Contributions of an Invitational Approach |journal=Journal of Invitational Theory & Practice |year=2022 |volume=20 |pages=38–60|doi=10.26522/jitp.v20i.3735 |s2cid=141888133 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

The Rapid Response: Facilitators and barriers to health care for lesbian, gay and bisexual (LGB) people. Toronto, ON: Ontario HIV Treatment Network; March 2014.</ref> Various bodies of literature have identified the health disparities associated with the LGBT community, and how these individuals receive disproportionate healthcare services. For example, mental health disorders such as depression and anxiety, eating disorders, obesity, and cardiovascular diseases are all of higher prevalence and a major concern amongst LGBT persons.<ref name=":14" /> These health issues are not sufficiently addressed either, as healthcare professionals (such as physicians) may be unaware of these individuals' sexual orientation. Another barrier that exists with regard to the healthcare disparities experienced by LGBT persons is the stigma that continues to persist in society. framework.<ref name=":33">{{Cite journal|last1=Gahagan|first1=Jacqueline|last2=Subirana-Malaret|first2=Montse|date=2018-06-13|title=Improving pathways to primary health care among LGBTQ populations addressing health issues predominantly affecting the LGBT community.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Makadon|first=Harvey J.|date=2011-04-01|title=Ending LGBT invisibility in health care: The first step in an increased risk of acute and chronic illness amongst LGBT persons.<ref name=":33" /> Research has also highlighted that higher rates of chronic illness seen in LGBT persons is associated with discrimination, minority stress, avoidance of healthcare providers, and irregular access to healthcare services.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity Data Collection in the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System|url=https://www.americanprogress.org/article/sexual-orientation-and-gender-identity-data-collection-in-the-behavioral-risk-factor-surveillance-system/|access-date=2021-12-06|website=Center for American Progress|date=March 29, 2016 |language=en}}</ref>

Another important consideration in addressing the quality of care received by the LGBT community is patient-physician communication.<ref name=":42">{{Cite journal|last1=Bonvicini|first1=Kathleen A|last2=Perlin|first2=Michael J|date=2003-10-01|title=The same but different: clinician–patient communication with gay and lesbian patients|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0738399102001891|journal=Patient Education and Counseling|language=en|volume=51|issue=2|pages=115–122|doi=10.1016/S0738-3991(02)00189-1|pmid=14572940|issn=0738-3991|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Many health risks LGBT persons face come as a result of avoidance and / or dissatisfaction of healthcare services; this is in part due to assumptions made by the patient's healthcare providers, such as assuming the sexuality of the patient and predicting their sexual behaviours.<ref name=":42" /> In these scenarios, it can be very difficult for LGBT persons to feel comfortable in a clinical setting because they may experience a decline in self-confidence and trust in their healthcare providers.

The underlying message in terms of providing equitable care, and access to care, for patients in the LGBT community is that healthcare providers and systems must be aware of the appropriate methods through which to administer care. The specific needs of LGBT persons must be appreciated in order to enhance the quality of care and provide it in a non-judgemental, gender-neutral manner.<ref name=":42" />

==== Immigrants ====
Inadequate access to primary care and treatment interventions has been and continues to be a prevalent issue amongst minority populations in Canada. As a result, many immigrants are faced with constant barriers with regard to receiving high-quality care. The patient experience is revered as one of the most significant aspects of healthcare, however its relation to immigrant status is not well defined.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lum|first1=Irene D.|last2=Swartz|first2=Rebecca H.|last3=Kwan|first3=Matthew Y.W.|date=May 2016|title=Accessibility and use of primary healthcare for immigrants living in the Niagara Region|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0277953616301241|journal=Social Science & Medicine|language=en|volume=156|pages=73–79|doi=10.1016/j.socscimed.2016.03.024|pmid=27017093|url-access=subscription}}</ref> The "healthy immigrant effect" is a term that recognizes how immigrants on average enter Canada with better health than those born in the country. However, over time, this health advantage experienced by immigrants may begin to decline.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=De Maio|first1=Fernando G.|last2=Kemp|first2=Eagan|date=2010|title=The deterioration of health status among immigrants to Canada|journal=Global Public Health|volume=5|issue=5|pages=462–478|doi=10.1080/17441690902942480|issn=1744-1706|pmid=19513909|s2cid=32380810}}</ref> Multiple factors contribute to this health decline, including: racialization and discrimination, stress of immigration, barriers accessing healthcare practitioners and others.<ref name=":0" />

The most prevalent barriers faced by immigrants with regard to accessing primary care services are related to geography and geographic distribution, language, and culture.<ref name=":03">{{Cite journal|last=Wang|first=Lu|date=2011-12-01|title=Analysing spatial accessibility to health care: a case study of access by different immigrant groups to primary care physicians in Toronto|journal=Annals of GIS|volume=17|issue=4|pages=237–251|doi=10.1080/19475683.2011.625975|bibcode=2011AnGIS..17..237W |s2cid=43781710|issn=1947-5683|doi-access=free}}</ref> Moreover, the distribution of physicians has a direct impact on the utilization of primary care services by immigrants. Immigrants tend to settle in suburbs, and long term immigrants tend to migrate toward suburban areas. These areas offer the most affordable housing options for immigrants, however this creates a "spatial mismatch"<ref name=":03" /> between patients and physicians since physicians and medical services are primarily concentrated in urban areas.<ref name=":03" />

Language is another strong barrier faced by immigrant populations due to the poor distribution of same-language physicians. Immigrants often face challenges in terms of understanding English medical terms.<ref name=":03" /> These linguistic differences are yet another contributing factor to the discordance and miscommunication between immigrants and English-speaking physicians.

Since healthcare services in Canada are paid in-part by the federal and provincial governments and by health insurance systems, economic and financial barriers are generally not considered to be a severe issue dealt with by the immigrant community. However, local availability (i.e., spatial accessibility<ref name=":03" />) of physicians and individual patient preferences such as ethnicity and language spoken by physicians are both impactful factors contributing to the precipitous decrease in primary healthcare access by immigrants.

Many immigrants report experiencing social isolation in Canada while also lacking social support from friends or family, which significantly impacts their mental health and also impacts their access to mental health services.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hynie |first1=Michaela |last2=Crooks |first2=Valorie A. |last3=Barragan |first3=Jackeline |date=December 2011 |title=Immigrant and refugee social networks: determinants and consequences of social support among women newcomers to Canada |journal=The Canadian Journal of Nursing Research |volume=43 |issue=4 |pages=26–46 |issn=0844-5621 |pmid=22435307}}</ref> Other racialized immigrants, specifically seniors, may be reluctant to access mental health services due to the stigmatization that surrounds these issues.<ref name=":12" /> Another significant barrier reported was the difficulty immigrants faced in finding mental health providers that were appropriately trained in cultural sensitivity.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Reitmanova |first1=Sylvia |last2=Gustafson |first2=Diana L. |date=October 2009 |title=Primary mental health care information and services for St. John's visible minority immigrants: gaps and opportunities |journal=Issues in Mental Health Nursing |volume=30 |issue=10 |pages=615–623 |doi=10.1080/01612840903033733 |issn=1096-4673 |pmid=19742371 |s2cid=23435565}}</ref>

Immigrants in Canada face multiple barriers to accessing mental health services.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Thomson|first1=Mary Susan|last2=Chaze|first2=Ferzana|last3=George|first3=Usha|last4=Guruge|first4=Sepali|date=December 2015|title=Improving Immigrant Populations' Access to Mental Health Services in Canada: A Review of name=":12">{{Cite journal|last1=Sadavoy|first1=Joel|last2=Meier|first2=Rosemary|last3=Ong|first3=Amoy Yuk Mui|date=March 2004|title=Barriers to access to mental health services for ethnic seniors: the journal|last1=Etowa|first1=Josephine|last2=Keddy|first2=Barbara|last3=Egbeyemi|first3=Julius|last4=Eghan|first4=Felicia|date=June 2007|title=Depression: the 'invisible grey fog' influencing the midlife health of African Canadian women|journal=International Journal of Mental Health Nursing|volume=16|issue=3|pages=203–213|doi=10.1111/j.1447-0349.2007.00469.x|issn=1445-8330|pmid=17535166}}</ref> Latin American men,<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2020-06-24|title=The Resettlement of |pages=101–111 |doi=10.25071/1920-7336.21335 |language=en-US|doi-access=free }}</ref> Iranian immigrants<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Jafari|first1=Siavash|last2=Baharlou|first2=Souzan|last3=Mathias|first3=Richard|date=February 2010|title=Knowledge of determinants of mental health among Iranian immigrants of BC, Another study conducted in Montreal examined the reasons behind why immigrants were reluctant to access mental health services. They found a multitude of reasons as to why immigrants were hesitant to seek help, including the fact that their perception of Western doctors' over willingness to utilize pharmaceutical medications, while they believed in the curative powers of non-pharmaceutical interventions, such as God and traditional folk medicine.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Whitley|first1=Rob|last2=Kirmayer|first2=Laurence J|last3=Groleau|first3=Danielle|date=2006-03-01|title=Understanding Immigrants' Reluctance to Use Mental Health Services: A Qualitative Study from Montreal|journal=The Canadian Journal of Psychiatry|language=en|volume=51|issue=4|pages=205–209|doi=10.1177/070674370605100401|pmid=16629344|s2cid=7737587|issn=0706-7437}}</ref>

==== Refugees ====
[[Refugee]]s in Canada experience numerous barriers to healthcare, such as gaps in knowledge regarding healthcare needs, which may not be always considered by public health initiatives and policies.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=McKeary |first=Marie |date=2010 |title=Barriers to Care: The Challenges for Canadian Refugees and their Health Care Providers |journal=Journal of Refugee Studies |volume=23 |issue=4 |pages=523–545 |doi=10.1093/jrs/feq038}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lane |first1=Ginny |last2=Farag |first2=Marwa |last3=White |first3=Judy |last4=Nisbet |first4=Christine |last5=Vatanparast |first5=Hassan |date=October 2018 |title=Chronic health disparities among refugee and immigrant children in Canada |journal=Applied Physiology, Nutrition, and Metabolism |volume=43 |issue=10 |pages=1043–1058 |doi=10.1139/apnm-2017-0407 |issn=1715-5320 |pmid=29726691 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Immigrants and refugees are among the groups most at risk for negative health effects resulting from persistent [[health disparities]]; differences in race, socioeconomic status, income, citizenship status, and other social factors further exacerbate healthcare inequalities. Compared to immigrants, refugees often require additional healthcare due to previous conditions in their countries of origin.<ref>{{Cite web |date=January 2017 |title=Promoting the health of refugees and migrants |url=https://www.who.int/migrants/about/framework_refugees-migrants.pdf |publisher=World Health Organization}}</ref>

The 2012 ''[[Protecting Canada's Immigration System Act]]'' formed a tiered system that classified refugees and separated care based on these classifications.<ref name=":1">{{Cite news |date=July 4, 2014 |title=Federal Court rules against government's cuts to refugee health program |url=https://torontosun.com/2014/07/04/federal-court-rules-against-governments-cuts-to-refugee-health-program/wcm/eeed07eb-1fb3-4c6c-bb80-1759c198e9b4 |access-date=March 10, 2019 |newspaper=Toronto Sun}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Levitz |first=Stephanie |date=January 26, 2015 |title=Current refugee health care system still violates court decision: advocates |url=https://www.ctvnews.ca/canada/article/current-refugee-health-care-system-still-violates-court-decision-advocates/ |access-date=March 10, 2019 |website=CTV News}}</ref> Differing levels of care were provided to refugees based on each refugee's home country and other factors.<ref name=":2" /> The act also reduced healthcare coverage for refugees provided by the Interim Federal Health Program (IFHP).<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Harris |first=Helen |date=2015 |title=Harming Refugee and Canadian Health: the Negative Consequences of Recent Reforms to Canada's Interim Federal Health Program |journal=Journal of International Migration and Integration |volume=16 |issue=4 |pages=1041–1055 |doi=10.1007/s12134-014-0385-x |s2cid=154626821}}</ref> The changes in refugee healthcare programs created in a rise in [[emergency room]] (ER) visits due to a lack of provisions of healthcare to refugees. This created concerns among Canadian citizens that the overall cost of healthcare will rise due. According to one study, the cuts to IFHP also made funding uncertain for programs that helped pay for ER costs.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Evans |first1=A. |last2=Caudarella |first2=A. |last3=Ratnapalan |first3=S. |last4=Chan |first4=K. |date=May 2014 |title=The Cost and Impact of the Interim Federal Health Program Cuts on Child Refugees in Canada |url=http://research.library.mun.ca/6441/3/The.Cost.and.Impact.pdf |journal=PLOS ONE |volume=9 |issue=5 |article-number=e96902 |bibcode=2014PLoSO...996902E |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0096902 |pmc=4014561 |pmid=24809676 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

In July 2014, Canada's Federal Court ruled that denying health services to asylum seekers was "cruel and unusual treatment" and therefore unconstitutional.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite book |url=https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2016/country-chapters/canada |title=World Report 2016: Rights Trends in Canada |date=January 6, 2016 |publisher=Human Rights Watch |chapter=Canada: Events of 2015 |access-date=March 10, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Ranalli |first=Audra |date=August 18, 2014 |title=Cuts to Refugee Health Care Found Unconstitutional: Canadian Doctors for Refugee Care v Canada |url=http://www.thecourt.ca/cuts-to-refugee-health-care-found-unconstitutional-canadian-doctors-for-refugee-care-v-canada/ |access-date=March 10, 2019 |website=TheCourt.ca}}</ref><ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite news |last=Fine |first=Sean |date=July 4, 2014 |title=Ottawa's refugee health-care cuts 'cruel and unusual,' court rules |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/ottawas-refugee-health-cuts-cruel-and-unusual-court-rules/article19459837/ |access-date=March 10, 2019 |work=The Globe and Mail}}</ref>

One study suggested open dialogue among policymakers, clinicians, and researchers and working with settlement programs to effectively respond to challenges encountered by the healthcare system regarding refugees.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last1=Pottie |first1=Kevin |last2=Gruner |first2=Doug |last3=Magwood |first3=Olivia |date=March 15, 2018 |title=Canada's response to refugees at the primary health care level |journal=Public Health Research & Practice |volume=28 |issue=1 |article-number=e2811803 |doi=10.17061/phrp2811803 |pmid=29582036 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The study notes that supporting primary care and focusing on social accountability training in medical schools will help ensure the sustainability of the healthcare system's response to refugees.<ref name=":3" />

==== People living with intellectual disabilities ====
Healthcare needs and comorbidities are often underdiagnosed in those living with intellectual disabilities.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Baxter|first1=Helen|last2=Lowe|first2=Kathy|last3=Houston|first3=Helen|last4=Jones|first4=Glyn|last5=Felce|first5=David|last6=Kerr|first6=Michael|date=February 2006|title=Previously unidentified morbidity in patients with intellectual disability|journal=The British Journal of General Practice|volume=56|issue=523|pages=93–98|issn=0960-1643|pmc=1828252|pmid=16464321}}</ref> A study conducted in Quebec, Canada investigated healthcare utilization and access amongst people with intellectual disabilities in comparison to the general population.<ref name=":05">{{Cite journal|last1=Maltais|first1=Julie|last2=Morin|first2=Diane|last3=Tassé|first3=Marc J.|date=May 2020|title=Healthcare services utilization among people with intellectual disability and comparison with the general population|journal=Journal of Applied Research in Intellectual Disabilities |volume=33|issue=3|pages=552–564|doi=10.1111/jar.12698|issn=1468-3148|pmid=32064737|s2cid=211136475}}</ref> Of the study sample, approximately 30 percent reported not having had a comprehensive medical examination in the past year, which is what is currently advised in the 2018 Canadian consensus guidelines for practitioners providing primary care for those with intellectual disabilities.<ref name=":05" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Sullivan|first1=William F.|last2=Diepstra|first2=Heidi|last3=Heng|first3=John|last4=Ally|first4=Shara|last5=Bradley|first5=Elspeth|last6=Casson|first6=Ian|last7=Hennen|first7=Brian|last8=Kelly|first8=Maureen|last9=Korossy|first9=Marika|last10=McNeil|first10=Karen|last11=Abells|first11=Dara|date=April 2018|title=Primary care of adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities: 2018 Canadian consensus guidelines|journal=Canadian Family Physician|volume=64|issue=4|pages=254–279|issn=1715-5258|pmc=5897068|pmid=29650602}}</ref>

Compared to the general population, women with intellectual disabilities aged 18–69 years were found to undergo cervical cancer screening less often. Results demonstrated them to be 1.5 times less likely to undergo a Pap test in the past three years compared to similar aged women without disabilities.<ref name=":05" /> For breast cancer screening, women living with severe or profound intellectual disabilities or [[Down syndrome]] were found to be screened significantly less than those in the general population.<ref name=":05" />

People with Down syndrome also reported the lowest usage of physiotherapy services compared to other measured population groups, which is a concern given that Down syndrome is associated with a variety of musculoskeletal problems that may be improved with physiotherapy.<ref name=":05" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Agarwal Gupta|first1=Neerja|last2=Kabra|first2=Madhulika|date=June 2014|title=Diagnosis and management of Down syndrome|journal=Indian Journal of Pediatrics|volume=81|issue=6|pages=560–567|doi=10.1007/s12098-013-1249-7|issn=0973-7693|pmid=24127006|s2cid=28986865}}</ref>

===Added incentive to encourage assisted suicide===
Canada since at least 2016 has legally allowed for a so-called [[Euthanasia in Canada|right to die]], or legalized [[euthanasia]].<ref name="Reason magazine, September 7th, 2022" /> The [[Associated Press]] reported in August, 2022 that, "...human rights advocates say the country's regulations lack necessary safeguards, devalue the lives of disabled people and are prompting doctors and health workers to suggest the procedure to those who might not otherwise consider it."<ref>{{cite web |last1=Cheng |first1=Maria |title='Disturbing': Experts troubled by Canada's euthanasia laws |url=https://apnews.com/article/covid-science-health-toronto-7c631558a457188d2bd2b5cfd360a867 |website=apnews.com |date=August 11, 2022 |publisher=Associated Press |access-date=9 September 2022}}</ref> Critics have raised concerns that doctors and medical professionals in Canada may have an added incentive to encourage patients to self-select an early or possibly even unnecessary instance of euthanasia as a cost cutting procedure due to governmental budget pressures based around a system of socialized medicine. Scott Shackford of ''[[Reason (magazine)|Reason]]'' magazine reported on September 7, 2022, that, "Unfortunately, the philosophical argument for the right to die can also end up colliding with troubling decisions in a country where the government funds and controls access to healthcare. That is reportedly happening in Canada, where some citizens say health officials are actively encouraging people with disabilities and other chronic medical issues to consider suicide."<ref name="Reason magazine, September 7th, 2022" />

==Canadians receiving healthcare in the United States==
Along with the highly publicized 2005 case of Shona Holmes, who campaigned against the Canadian healthcare system on behalf of the Americans for Prosperity's PAC from 2009 through 2012, there have been other high-profiled incidents in which Canadian politicians have visited the Mayo Clinic and other highly specialized hospitals in the United States. Media reports about [[Robert Bourassa]], the premier of Quebec in 1994, then Prime Minister [[Jean Chrétien]]'s visit to the Mayo Clinic in 1999,<ref name="gazette20100203"/> then Liberal MP [[Belinda Stronach]]'s visit to the Mayo in 2007, and then Newfoundland and Labrador Premier [[Danny Williams (Canadian politician)|Danny Williams]] have been criticized for being cynical, ironic, hypocritical, and / or elitist.<ref name="levant20020115"/><ref name="CTV_20070914"/><ref name="theindependent_1994"/><ref name="CBC_20100202"/>

An often-cited 2002 study reported in the ''Health Affairs'' journal, said that their research results did "not support the widespread perception that Canadian residents seek care extensively in the United States."<ref name="Katz2002">{{Cite journal |last1=Katz |first1=S. J. |last2=Cardiff |first2=K. |last3=Pascali |first3=M. |last4=Barer |first4=M. L. |last5=Evans |first5=R. G. |year=2002 |title=Phantoms in the Snow: Canadians' Use of Health Care Services in the United States |journal=Health Affairs |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=19–31 |doi=10.1377/hlthaff.21.3.19 |pmid=12025983|doi-access=free }}</ref> The Katz study—based on an analysis of data from the 1996–1997 National Population Health Survey (NPHS)—a large survey representative of the Canadian noninstitutionalized population, including 17,276 Canadian residents, reported that 0.5% sought medical care in the U.S. in the previous year. Of these, less than a quarter had travelled to the U.S. expressly to get that care.<ref name="Katz2002"/> This was supported by an additional analysis performed from the American side, using a structured telephone survey of all ambulatory care clinical facilities located in specific heavily populated U.S. urban corridors bordering Canada and discharge data for 1994–1998 from major border states, and contacted key informants at each of ''[[U.S. News & World Report]]'''s "America's Best Hospitals" to inquire about the number of Canadians seen in both inpatient and outpatient settings.<ref name=Katz2002/> The authors characterized this rate of medical travel as "barely detectable relative to the use of care by Canadians at home" and that the results "do not support the widespread perception that Canadian residents seek care extensively in the United States."<ref name=Katz2002/> The majority of Canadians who seek healthcare in the U.S. are already there for other reasons, including business travel or vacations.<ref name="Katz2002"/> A smaller proportion seek care in the U.S. for reasons of confidentiality, including abortions, mental illness, substance abuse, and other problems that they may not wish to divulge to their local physician, family, or employer. Canadians offered free care in the U.S. paid by the Canadian government have sometimes declined it.<ref name="Schmitz_1991">{{Cite news |url=http://www.healthadvocates.info/HealthAssurance.pdf |title=Health Assurance |last=Schmitz |first=Anthony |date=January–February 1991 |work=In Health |issue=1 |volume=5 |pages=39–47}}</ref>

==Portability and provincial residency requirements==
The ''Canada Health Act'' covers residents of Canada, which are persons "lawfully entitled to be or to remain in Canada who makes his home and is ordinarily present in the province, but does not include a tourist, a transient or a visitor to the province."<ref name="Government of Canada">{{Cite web |url=http://www.hc-sc.gc.ca/hcs-sss/medi-assur/faq-eng.php#a2 |title=Canada Health Act - Frequently Asked Questions |date=May 16, 2005 |publisher=Government of Canada |access-date=February 1, 2015}}</ref> When traveling within Canada, a Canadian's health card from his or her home province or territory is accepted for hospital and physician services.<ref name="Government of Canada" />

Each province has residency and physical presence requirements to qualify for health care coverage. For example, to qualify for coverage in Ontario, with certain exceptions, one must be physically present in Ontario for 153 days in any given 12-month period. Most provinces require 183 days of physical presence in any given 12-month period. Exceptions may be made for mobile workers, if the individual can provide documentation from his or her employer verifying that the individual's work requires frequent travel in and out of the province.<ref name="Queen">{{Cite web |url=http://www.health.gov.on.ca/en/public/publications/ohip/travel_another_province_territory.aspx |title=Studying, Working or Travelling to Another Province or Territory Within Canada |publisher=Queen's Printer for Ontario |access-date=February 1, 2015}}</ref> Transients, self-employed itinerant workers (e.g. farm workers) who move from province to province several times within a year, and peripatetic retired or unemployed individuals who move from province to province (e.g. staying with various relatives, or living in a recreational vehicle) may find themselves ineligible for health coverage in any province or territory, even though they are Canadian citizens or landed immigrants physically present in Canada 365 days a year. "[[Snowbird (person)|Snowbirds]]" (Canadians who winter in warm climates) and other Canadians who are out their home province or territory for a total of more than 183 days in twelve months lose all coverage, which is reinstated after a three-month waiting period.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.hc-sc.gc.ca/hcs-sss/medi-assur/faq-eng.php#a11 |title=How do I resume my health care coverage when returning to Canada following a lengthy absence? |date=May 16, 2005 |publisher=Government of Canada |access-date=February 1, 2015}}</ref> Students attending a university or college outside their home province are generally covered by the health insurance program of their home province, however, "Typically this coverage (while out-of-province but within Canada) is for physician and hospital services only."<ref name="Queen" /> The Ontario Ministry of Health and Long Term Care, for example, states, "Therefore, when travelling outside of Ontario but within Canada, the ministry recommends that you obtain private supplementary health insurance for non-physician / non-hospital services."<ref name="Queen" /> Such services might include prescription drugs, or ground and air ambulance services that might be covered in one's home province.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.hc-sc.gc.ca/hcs-sss/medi-assur/faq-eng.php#a8 |title=Do I need private health care coverage when travelling within Canada? |date=May 16, 2005 |publisher=Government of Canada |access-date=February 1, 2015}}</ref>

==Comparison to selected other countries==
{{Main|Comparison of Canadian and American health care systems}}

The Canadian health care system is often [[Canadian and American health care systems compared|compared]] to the U.S. system. According to a report by the New York-based independent health-care advocacy group, The Commonwealth Fund, that compared 11 rich countries, over 25% of Canadians report a [[body-mass index]] of 30 or higher—a measure of obesity—compared to 40% in the U.S. This is twice the rate reported in Norway, Sweden, and Switzerland.<ref name="NaPo_Perkel_20200131">{{Cite news| last = Perkel| first = Colin| title = Canada lags behind peers in doctors per capita, but average in physician visits| work = The National Post| access-date = January 9, 2021| date = January 31, 2020| url = https://nationalpost.com/pmn/news-pmn/canada-news-pmn/canada-lags-behind-peers-in-doctors-per-capita-but-average-in-physician-visits}}</ref> Canada ranked 4th in the eleven countries for the number of suicides per 100,000 compared, with a rate of 11.8 per 100,000 compared to the U.S. rate of 13.9 which was the highest of the eleven wealthy countries. From 2000 to 2015, the number of preventable deaths caused by treatable health conditions—diabetes, high blood pressure or some cancers—dropped from 109 to 72 deaths per 100,000.<ref name="NaPo_Perkel_20200131"/> In 2016, of the eleven countries, the U.S. "had the highest rate of avoidable deaths at 112 per 100,000".<ref name="NaPo_Perkel_20200131"/>

British Columbia – BC Injury Law| date = October 17, 2016| access-date = 2020-09-10| url = https://bc-injury-law.com/tag/cambie-surgeries-corporation-v-british-columbia/}}</ref> Day was quoted in the 2006 ''Times'' saying, without evidence, that, "This is a country in which dogs can get a hip replacement in under a week and in which humans can wait two to three years."<ref name="NYT_Krauss_2006"/> The Canadian Health Coalition responded to Day's claims, pointing out that "access to veterinary care for animals is based on the ability to pay. Dogs are put down if their owners can't pay. Access to care should not be based on ability to pay."<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.healthcoalition.ca/DayFactCheck.pdf |title=Fact Check |access-date=February 17, 2009}}{{dead link|date=June 2016|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref>

According to a May 1, 2006 ''Maclean's'' in-depth article, private medical providers in British Columbia and Quebec were expanding their services encouraged by the Supreme Court's 2005 ''Chaoulli v. Quebec'' ruling. Quebec was influenced by the success of the blend of private and public healthcare services in France, and Brian Day was influenced by similar health services in New Zealand.<ref name="macleans_Shimo_20060501">{{Cite magazine| last = Shimo| first = Alexandra| title = Private Medical Care in Canada| magazine = Maclean's| series = The Complete Archive| access-date = October 16, 2020| date = May 1, 2006| url = https://archive.macleans.ca/search?QueryTerm=healthcare%20canada| archive-date = October 18, 2020| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20201018022533/https://archive.macleans.ca/search?QueryTerm=healthcare%20canada}}</ref> ''Maclean's'' provided a consumer guide to private healthcare services in 2006.

In 2009, the [[Canadian Medical Association]] met to discuss the potential for an increase in private clinics in Canada's healthcare system A European study presented at the meeting was "expected to call for private clinics, such as the chain of radiology centres owned by Ouellet, to play a bigger role in Canada's health-care system."<ref name="thestar_Laidlaw_20090812"/>

== Canadian healthcare contribution to Climate Change ==
Climate change is a growing concern all around the world, and its causes vary from multiple factors. It has been identified that Climate change is the single greatest public health threat of the 21st century.<ref name=":16">{{Cite journal |last1=Eckelman |first1=Matthew J. |last2=Sherman |first2=Jodi D. |last3=MacNeill |first3=Andrea J. |date=2018-07-31 |editor-last=Patz |editor-first=Jonathan Alan |title=Life cycle environmental emissions and health damages from the Canadian healthcare system: An economic-environmental-epidemiological analysis |journal=PLOS Medicine |language=en |volume=15 |issue=7 |article-number=e1002623 |doi=10.1371/journal.pmed.1002623 |doi-access=free |issn=1549-1676 |pmc=6067712 |pmid=30063712}}</ref> The healthcare sector in Canada contributes to climate change, and it was responsible for 4.6% of national greenhouse gas emission in 2009 to 2015.<ref name=":16" /><ref name=":08">{{Cite journal |last=Mercer |first=Caroline |date=2019-04-07 |title=How health care contributes to climate change |journal=Canadian Medical Association Journal |volume=191 |issue=14 |pages=E403–E404 |doi=10.1503/cmaj.109-5722 |pmid=30962202 |pmc=6453681 |issn=0820-3946}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Tochkin |first1=Jeff |last2=Richmond |first2=John |last3=Hertelendy |first3=Attila |date=2023 |title=Healthcare system leadership and climate change: five lessons for improving health systems resiliency |url=https://bmjleader.bmj.com/lookup/doi/10.1136/leader-2021-000583 |journal=BMJ Leader |language=en |volume=7 |issue=1 |pages=52–55 |doi=10.1136/leader-2021-000583 |pmid=37013877 |issn=2398-631X}}</ref> With the relationship between air pollution and human health, it was estimated by researchers that "every year, health care emissions result in {{val|23000}} years of life lost due to disability or early death".<ref name=":08" />

The health sector has contributed to pollution in various ways, with Hospitals and Pharmaceutical companies as the largest drivers of its emissions according to the PLOS Medicine study. There is also the impact of medical waste, anesthetics used in surgery, and unsustainable materials which are all greenhouse gases.<ref name=":08" /><ref name=":16" />

There have been projects led by The Canadian Coalition for Green Health Care with the aim to reduce the environmental impacts of providing healthcare, such as reducing toxic chemicals when cleaning and promoting sustainable foods in hospitals.<ref name=":08" /> They recently studied medical imaging equipment's energy consumption.<ref name=":08" /> When patients and hospital staff travel to hospitals and clinics they release greenhouse gas, which can be viewed as part of the equation.<ref name=":08" /><ref name=":16" />

== Potential future impact of Climate Change on health ==
[[Climate change]] is affecting the health of Canadians today and the projected future impacts are even greater.<ref name=":8">{{Cite web |last=Canada |first=Health |date=2022-01-24 |title=Risks to health from climate change |url=https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/climate-change-health/risks-to-health.html |access-date=2025-09-22 |website=www.canada.ca}}</ref> The geographical size and climate diversity of Canada contributes to the complexity of understanding the effects of climate on health. It is important to understand climate change related risks to health in order to consider future impacts. Risks can be thought about in two categories, indirect and direct.<ref name=":8" /> Direct risks are related to climate exposure events such as but not limited to floods, storms and heat waves. Indirect risks are related to social and environmental causes. For example, changes in migration patterns, impacts on personal economy leading to poverty, erosion of culture and more. Health risks and impacts related to climate change can either be short term or last for a few months or be long term and irreversible. For example, a short-term impact could be heat stroke / illness, whereas the mental health impacts of a weather incident could last for many months. A long term and irreversible impact is the cultural erosion for indigenous people.<ref name=":8" /> There are five key categories of climate related risks that have been identified by the [[Government of Canada|Canadian government]]. These include; water-related natural hazards, water quality and security, food safety and security, air quality and mental health impacts of climate change.<ref name=":8" />

In 2022 a report titled "[https://changingclimate.ca/health-in-a-changing-climate/ Health in a Changing Climate]," was published with a comprehensive overview of the current and projected impacts of climate change on health for Canadians.<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |title=Health of Canadians in a Changing Climate — Advancing our Knowledge for Action |url=https://changingclimate.ca/health-in-a-changing-climate/ |access-date=2025-09-22}}</ref> This is the first report of its kind in Canada and is an assessment to bring a broader understanding to government, health officials and individuals who are thinking about and planning for increased impact of climate change on health. One of the key recommendations coming out of the report is the importance of adaptation of health systems and society to mitigate health impacts of climate change. [https://www.cma.ca/ The Canadian Medical Association] has issued a report with six recommendations on [https://www.canada.ca/en/services/environment/weather/climatechange/climate-plan/national-adaptation-strategy/full-strategy.html Canada's First National Adaptation Strategy] that are directly health related.<ref name=":10">{{Cite web |title=PDF.js viewer |url=https://policybase.cma.ca/viewer?file=%2Fmedia%2FBriefPDF%2FBR2022-15.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240208104034/https://policybase.cma.ca/viewer?file=%2Fmedia%2FBriefPDF%2FBR2022-15.pdf |archive-date=2024-02-08 |access-date=2025-09-22 |website=policybase.cma.ca}}</ref><ref name=":11">{{Cite web |last=Canada |first=Natural Resources |date=2008-08-12 |title=Climate change adaptation in Canada |url=https://natural-resources.canada.ca/climate-change/climate-change-adaptation |access-date=2025-09-22 |website=natural-resources.canada.ca}}</ref> Climate change adaptation refers to the ability of a society to reduce negative impacts of climate change and to take advantage of potential opportunities building resilience to climate change.<ref name=":11" /> Many organizing bodies in Canada are in agreement that adaptation is key to mitigating climate change health impacts.<ref name=":9" /><ref name=":17">{{Cite web |title=The health costs of climate change |url=https://climateinstitute.ca/reports/the-health-costs-of-climate-change/ |access-date=2025-09-22 |website=Canadian Climate Institute |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":10" />

Distribution of health impacts is important for [[Climate change adaptation|adaptation strategies]]. According to the [https://climateinstitute.ca/ Canadian Climate Institute] impacts on health are directly related to [[Social determinants of health|the social determinants of health]].<ref name=":17" /> Which means that the impact of climate change on health is not and will not be equitably distributed in the future. Those who have higher rates of exposure, are more vulnerable and have lower capacity to adapt will be more negatively impacted.<ref name=":17" /> An important factor to consider for the future is that the [[health equity]] gap in Canada is widening and climate change impacts are anticipated to widen that gap even further.<ref name=":17" />
== Systemic challenges and policy response ==

In January 2025, Health Minister Mark Holland issued a formal statement underscoring that Canadians are facing significant systemic challenges within publicly funded healthcare, including:<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |last=Canada |first=Health |date=2025-01-10 |title=Statement from the Minister of Health on the Canada Health Act |url=https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/news/2025/01/statement-from-the-minister-of-health-on-the-canada-health-act.html |access-date=2025-06-23 |website=www.canada.ca}}</ref>
* Overcrowded emergency departments (EDs), leading to prolonged wait times and increased strain on acute-care facilities.  
* A shortage of primary care providers, leaving many Canadians without access to a family doctor or nurse practitioner.  
* Health-care workforce burnout, as existing staff are stretched thin across the system.

As a response, the federal government negotiated historic bilateral agreements with provinces and territories worth $200 billion over ten years, targeting:<ref name=":7" />
* Enhanced access to family health services.
* Reduction of surgical and diagnostic procedure backlogs.
* Investment in modernizing healthcare infrastructure.

The launch of the Canadian Dental Care Plan (CDCP) - the first universal dental benefit - has already served over 1.2 million Canadians lacking coverage, aiming to reduce avoidable long-term health burdens.<ref name=":7" /> Alongside this, the federal pharmacare rollout makes key diabetes drugs and contraceptives freely available to reduce financial barriers to essential medications.

A central policy development - the "CHA Services Policy", announced in an interpretation letter dated January 10, 2025—expands the definition of insured "medically necessary" services to include those administered by nurse practitioners, pharmacists, midwives, and other regulated providers starting April 1, 2026.<ref name=":7" /> Any patient charges for those services will be classified as extra-billing, subject to Canada's Health Act penalties if not addressed. The policy also mandates reporting of patient charges by December 2028, with the potential for federal funding deductions from non-compliant provinces.

However, commentators describe this reinterpretation as ambiguous and limited - it refrains from expanding the core basket of services and fails to define "medically necessary" in legislation; it also does not regulate services outside the public system, such as private virtual clinics or non‑CHA providers.<ref name=":7" /> The policy's legal robustness has also been questioned due to the non-binding nature of interpretation letters under the CHA framework.

While these reforms reflect a federal push to address clear weaknesses - ER overcrowding, primary-care access, workforce capacity, dental and pharmacare coverage, and unchecked private billing - their success depends on federal-provincial collaboration, regulatory precision, and enforcement strength under the Canada Health Act.<ref name=":7" />

extract:
Healthcare in Canada is delivered through the provincial and territorial systems of publicly funded single-payer healthcare, informally called Medicare. It is guided by the provisions of the Canada Health Act, adopted during 1984, and is universal. The 2002 Royal Commission, known as the Romanow Report, revealed that Canadians consider universal access to publicly funded health services as a "fundamental value that ensures national health care insurance for everyone wherever they live in the country".
Canadian Medicare provides coverage for approximately 70 percent of Canadians' healthcare needs, and the remaining 30 percent is paid for through the private sector. The 30 percent typically relates to services not covered or only partially covered by Medicare, such as prescription drugs, eye care, medical devices, gender care, psychotherapy, physical therapy and dentistry. About 65-75 percent of Canadians have some form of supplementary health insurance related to the aforementioned reasons; many receive it through their employers or use secondary social programs related to extended coverage for families receiving social assistance or vulnerable demographics, such as seniors, minors, and those with disabilities.
According to the Canadian Institute for Health Information (CIHI), by 2019, Canada's aging population represents an increase in healthcare costs of approximately one percent a year, which is a modest increase. In a 2020 Statistics Canada Canadian Perspectives Survey Series (CPSS), 69 percent of Canadians self-reported that they had excellent or very good physical health—an improvement from 60 percent in 2018. In 2019, 80 percent of Canadian adults self-reported having at least one major risk factor for chronic disease: smoking, physical inactivity, unhealthy eating, or excessive alcohol use. Canada has one of the highest rates of adult obesity among Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries attributing to approximately 2.7 million cases of diabetes (types 1 and 2 combined). Four chronic diseases—cancer (a leading cause of death), cardiovascular diseases, respiratory diseases and diabetes account for 65 percent of deaths in Canada. There are approximately 8 million individuals aged 15 and older with one or more disabilities in Canada.
In 2021, the Canadian Institute for Health Information reported that healthcare spending reached $308 billion, or 12.7 percent of Canada's GDP for that year. In 2022 Canada's per-capita spending on health expenditures ranked 12th among healthcare systems in the OECD. Canada has performed close to the average on the majority of OECD health indicators since the early 2000s, and ranks above average for access to care, but the number of doctors and hospital beds are considerably below the OECD average. The Commonwealth Funds 2021 report comparing the healthcare systems of 11 high-income countries ranked Canada second-to-last. Identified weaknesses of Canada's system were comparatively higher infant mortality rate, the prevalence of chronic conditions, long wait times, poor availability of after-hours care, and a lack of prescription drugs coverage. An increasing problem in Canada's health system is a shortage of healthcare professionals and hospital capacity.
